habitat: Shaded hill streams, evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, moist valleys, forest edges near water and ravines. Strongly tied to flowing water across the Western Ghats. Near-endemic: beyond the Western Ghats it occurs only in the Satpuras, at Mount Abu and in parts of the Eastern Ghats.

description.adult_male: Large, glossy dark blue-black thrush with intense electric-blue patches on shoulders, scapulars and sometimes forehead. Plumage shines differently under varying light, shifting from deep blackish-blue to metallic cobalt. Bill strong and dark; legs dark grey. Eyes deep-set, giving a bold expression.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike; females are at most marginally duller, with the blue patches on forehead and shoulders slightly less extensive. Structure and proportions identical.
description.juvenile: Duller sooty-brown overall with faint mottling on breast and flanks. Blue patches largely absent or muted. Wings and scapulars may show slight bluish sheen as the bird matures. Bill and legs paler than adults.
description.in_flight: Strong, direct flight low over streams or through forest corridors. Blue shoulder patches flash as wings open. Tail slightly rounded; flight usually between favoured perches along watercourses.

behaviour: Often seen near forest streams, hopping from boulders to roots and inspecting wet leaf litter for prey. Extremely vocal at dawn and dusk; famous for its rich, fluty, human-like whistled phrases that carry far through forest valleys. Also produces sharp metallic 'tink' notes. Will sit motionless on shaded perches for long periods before dropping to forage. Territorial males sing from exposed rocks or low branches near water. Nests typically constructed in crevices of banks, behind waterfalls or on rock ledges above streams.
food: Insects, larvae, snails, crabs, small amphibians and other streamside prey. Regularly flips leaves and probes crevices for invertebrates; occasionally takes small fish or tadpoles.

photos.caption: Adult near a shaded stream at Mangaon, Raigad.

did_you_know: Its rambling, human-like whistling, often started in the half-light before dawn, earned it the old colonial nickname 'Whistling Schoolboy'.

habitat: Dense undergrowth in moist evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, bamboo thickets, shaded plantations, and well-vegetated gullies. Prefers dense, tangled understory with low perches and concealed pathways.

description.adult_male: Striking shama with glossy black head, mantle and upperparts; bright chestnut belly and flanks; very long black tail with white outer feathers and a conspicuous white rump patch that flares in flight. Eyes dark and expressive. Posture upright and alert, often flicking tail.
description.adult_female: Duller and browner than the male. Upperparts grey-brown to olive-brown; belly pale rufous to buff; tail shorter and less dramatic. White rump less boldly contrasted. Lacks the male's deep glossy black sheen.
description.juvenile: Heavily scaled or mottled above and below with rich brown and buff spotting. Tail short; white rump indistinct. Gradually transitions into adult plumage over several months, with young males beginning to show darker head and longer tail feathers first.
description.in_flight: Fluid and agile flight through dense undergrowth. White rump and outer tail feathers flash distinctly when the tail spreads during short flights or while landing. Frequently flicks long tail downward as it lands on low perches.

behaviour: Elusive and shy, usually staying low inside tangles or bamboo clumps. Despite being hard to see, it is among the finest songsters of the region: rich, melodious, fluty phrases delivered from a hidden perch, often at dawn. Males also mimic other birds. Forages on or near the ground, hopping quietly between shadows for insects. Territorial males sing year-round but intensify during breeding season. When alarmed, adopts an erect posture and flicks its long tail sharply. Nests in tree cavities, bamboo hollows or crevices, lined with roots and leaves.
food: Primarily insects – beetles, termites, ants, caterpillars, grasshoppers and small invertebrates. Occasionally takes small berries and fruits.

photos.caption: Adult male showing long tail and bold white rump.
Female white-rumped shama perched in foliage.

did_you_know: The White-rumped Shama is one of India’s finest mimics: males can weave calls of barbets, drongos and sunbirds seamlessly into their own song.

habitat: Gardens, orchards, coffee and tea plantations, village edges, forest edges and clearings, scrub, and urban parks. Closely associated with shrubs and small trees, especially where fruiting plants and hedges are present.

description.adult_male: Slender brown bulbul with a distinctive pointed black crest and prominent white cheeks. A bright red 'whisker' patch behind the eye contrasts with the white cheek and dark head. Upperparts warm brown; underparts whitish with a darker brown breast. Vent and undertail coverts bright red. Tail fairly long and dark with white tips to the outer feathers. Bill and legs dark; eye dark.
description.adult_female: Plumage essentially identical to male; sexes alike in the field with the same black crest, red whisker patch, red vent and white-tipped tail. Slightly smaller on average but not reliably distinguishable.
description.juvenile: Crest shorter and browner; red whisker patch and vent duller or partially developed. Underparts buffier, with less contrast between breast and belly. Overall appearance softer and less crisp than adults, often with a faint gape and more hesitant movements.
description.in_flight: Flight typically consists of short, direct bursts between perches, with shallow wingbeats and a slightly undulating path. In flight, the white tips to the tail and the red vent can stand out, especially when the tail is fanned on landing.

behaviour: Usually seen in pairs or small family groups, often perched conspicuously on wires, shrub tops and exposed branches. Highly vocal, with a variety of ringing whistles, chattering notes and characteristic repeated phrases, often delivered from a prominent song perch. Frequently flicks tail and adjusts crest while calling. Forages in shrubs and small trees for fruit and insects, and also descends to the ground for fallen fruit. Nests are shallow cup nests placed in bushes or small trees, often close to human habitation. Bold and adaptable around people, commonly seen in gardens and plantations throughout the Sahyadris.
food: Primarily fruits and berries (including figs and cultivated fruits); also takes insects, small invertebrates, flower buds and nectar. Often feeds in mixed flocks at fruiting trees.

photos.caption: Palakkad, Kerala.

did_you_know: Introduced populations now thrive from Florida to Mauritius and Australia, descended from escaped cage birds.

habitat: Tall evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, forest edges, mid- to upper-canopy layers. Often follows mixed-species bird flocks and frequents clearings within dense forests.

description.adult_male: Glossy black, highly iridescent in sunlight with bluish-green sheen. Prominent recurved crest on forehead. Extremely long tail streamers ending in distinctive spoon-shaped 'rackets' – the species’ signature feature. Strong, slightly hooked bill and bright red eyes.
description.adult_female: Similar to male, with slightly duller gloss and often shorter or narrower tail streamers. Crest may appear less pronounced.
description.juvenile: Duller sooty black with little or no iridescence. Crest absent or minimal. Tail streamers short or undeveloped; 'rackets' not yet formed. Iris dark brown.
description.in_flight: Long tail streamers trail dramatically, twisting during turns. Flashy silhouette with broad wings and characteristic undulating flight through canopy gaps.

behaviour: A bold, intelligent forest bird. Famous for exceptional mimicry – copies alarm calls, songs, and even mammal noises. Regular leader species in mixed hunting flocks, using its mimicked alarm calls to influence flock movement. Feeds actively by sallying for insects from exposed canopy perches or following mammals for disturbed prey. Aggressive towards predators and larger birds; known to chase raptors from territory. Crest raised when excited or during vocal displays.
food: Large flying insects, beetles, winged termites, small lizards, nectar, and occasionally fledglings or small birds. Often captures insects in aerial sallies.

photos.caption: A boisterous bird. This one is calm, though: Kannur, Kerala

did_you_know: Its mimicry is so advanced that it can imitate alarm calls of multiple species to manipulate mixed flocks for its own feeding advantage.

habitat: Open scrub, cultivated fields, hedgerows, forest edges, dry grasslands and semi-open areas with scattered bushes or small trees. Frequently uses human-modified landscapes.

description.adult_male: Ashy-grey crown and nape, striking black mask through eye to ear coverts, rich rufous back and rump, and a bold white wing patch. Underparts pale buff. Long black tail with white outer edges. Variation across subspecies: some populations show blacker heads or deeper rufous mantles.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike; females are at most very slightly duller, with the mask and rufous tones a little less intense.
description.juvenile: Warm buff-brown with fine barring on upperparts and flanks. Weak mask. Shorter tail, yellowish gape. Gradual loss of barring with age.
description.in_flight: White wing patch and rufous mantle flash distinctly. Flight low and direct with rapid wingbeats; often glides between exposed perches.

behaviour: Bold and highly territorial bird, also known as the Rufous-backed Shrike. Hunts from exposed perches such as wires, poles, or prominent twigs. Classic shrike behaviour includes impaling prey on thorns or barbed wire ('larders'), used for storage and mating displays. Calls include clear whistles, harsh 'shak-shak', chatters and scolding notes, and it is a skilled mimic of other birds. Pairs defend territories vigorously, especially in breeding season. Frequently patrols open fields for prey.
food: Large insects, grasshoppers, beetles, caterpillars, lizards, small rodents, and occasionally small birds. Uses perch-to-ground sallying and ambush techniques.

photos.caption: Standing tall: a rufous-backed shrike in an upright posture.

did_you_know: Shrikes are sometimes called 'butcher birds' because they impale prey on thorns or barbed wire. These grisly larders may help them handle prickly or toxic prey such as hairy caterpillars, allowing the prey to dry out before being eaten.

habitat: Tall grasses in marshes, wet meadows, paddy margins, open country near water, and seasonally wet grasslands. Usually stays low but emerges to sing.

description.adult_male: Very small brown warbler. Breeding plumage: bright golden-orange crown contrasting with brown streaked upperparts, short rounded tail, and creamy underparts. Non-breeding male: crown dull brown and heavily streaked; tail becomes longer, giving a different silhouette.
description.adult_female: Resembles non-breeding male: less bright crown, longer tail, and slightly paler below. Subtler overall colours.
description.juvenile: Buff and brown with streaked upperparts; lacks bright golden crown. Underparts warm buff with diffuse streaks. Appears softer-toned and more rounded.
description.in_flight: Short, fluttery flight above grass-tops. Breeding males rise briefly for display flights, hovering with buzzing calls; short tail makes the bird appear more compact.

behaviour: The bright-capped cisticola, also called the golden-headed cisticola, becomes conspicuous when singing. Males sing repetitive 'teewip' or buzzing notes from exposed grass stems. Performs display flights – spiralling upward then parachuting down while singing. Forages low within grasses, picking insects from stems. Builds elaborate sewn nests using grass and spider silk; dome-shaped with side entrance.
food: Small insects and larvae, spiders and other invertebrates gleaned from tall grass stems and leaves.

photos.caption: The Cisticola exilis exilis.

did_you_know: This tiny grassland warbler changes its look dramatically between seasons: in the breeding season it has a short tail and glowing golden crown, while in the non-breeding season the tail becomes much longer and the crown duller, so much so that inexperienced observers often think they are seeing two different species.

habitat: Open scrub, dry deciduous forest, secondary woodland, village edges, gardens, orchards and parks. Readily adapts to semi-urban and agricultural landscapes.

description.adult_male: Dull brownish-grey overall with a slightly streaked forehead and throat, pale greyish underparts and a stout yellowish bill. Iris pale yellow to whitish, giving a 'staring' expression. Feathers loosely arranged, giving a scruffy appearance typical of the species.
description.adult_female: Indistinguishable from male in the field; sexes share identical plumage, size and behaviour.
description.juvenile: Fluffier and paler than adults with less defined streaking, duller grey-brown tone and a bright yellow gape. Iris darker than adults. Juveniles stay close to the group, following adults and giving persistent food-begging calls.
description.in_flight: Short, low, and noisy flights with wings and tail fanned. Typical movement is a series of fluttering hops between bushes or along the ground. Flocks keep tightly together while calling.

behaviour: Exceptionally social, usually found in cohesive groups of 6–10+ birds, giving rise to the nickname 'Seven Sisters'. Engages in cooperative breeding: several group members assist in incubation, feeding nestlings and defending territories. Frequent allopreening and allogrooming reinforce social bonds. Forages mostly on the ground, turning over leaf litter for insects and fallen fruits. Sentinels take elevated positions and give rasping alarm calls. Constant contact chatter keeps the flock coordinated. Roosts communally in dense shrubbery or low trees.
food: Wide-ranging diet including insects, beetles, ants, termites, caterpillars, seeds, berries, small fruits and occasional human food scraps. Will opportunistically take small lizards or frogs when available.

photos.caption: A Jungle Babbler perched at Mangaon, Raigad.
Individual from Kawal Wildlife Sanctuary, Andhra Pradesh.
A pair interacting after monsoon rain in Chalakudy, Kerala.

did_you_know: Jungle Babblers breed cooperatively: besides the parents, other group members help feed and guard the chicks, which is why a single nest can have half a dozen attendants.

habitat: Flowering gardens, orchards, hedges, groves, scrub, open woodland, forest edges, coffee plantations and urban parks. Closely associated with flowering shrubs and trees including hibiscus, bottlebrush and ornamental species.

description.adult_male: Very small, intensely coloured sunbird. Crown and nape glossy metallic green; mantle, back and sides of head dark maroon; throat iridescent violet-purple above a maroon breast band; shoulder patch metallic green. Rump metallic purple, usually hidden by the folded wings. Belly pale yellow, flanks and undertail whitish. Bill thin, decurved and black.
description.adult_female: Much duller than male: upperparts grey-brown to olive-brown; throat greyish-white, breast and belly yellow; faint pale eyebrow; wings brownish. Tail blackish with white tips to the outer feathers, sometimes visible in flight.
description.juvenile: Resembles the adult female but even duller; brownish-olive above and washed-out yellow below. Bill shorter and paler at base. Lacks the clean contrasts of adults and shows faint gape flanges. Young males begin showing dull maroon tones on throat as they mature.
description.in_flight: Fast, buzzing, and highly agile flight with rapid wingbeats. Frequently darts between flowers in short bursts. Capable of brief hovering, though usually perches to feed. In backlit conditions the male’s purple rump and green crown flash conspicuously.

behaviour: Restless, energetic and constantly moving among flowers. Often hangs upside down to reach deep corollas. Males sing a rapid, high twittering from exposed perches and chase rivals from rich nectar sources, sometimes taking on larger birds. The female builds the nest and incubates alone; the male guards the territory. Nest is a delicate hanging purse with a side entrance, woven from plant fibres, cobwebs and lichens. Calls include sharp 'chip' notes.
food: Primarily nectar from flowering shrubs and trees; also takes insects, small spiders and caterpillars, especially during breeding to feed young. Opportunistically gleans insects from foliage.

photos.caption: The male of the species, spotted in Goa.
A female purple-rumped sunbird.

did_you_know: The purple-rumped sunbird’s nest is an architectural marvel: a tiny hanging pouch stitched together with cobwebs. Birds often steal spider silk directly from webs – and sometimes from spiders still sitting in them – to get the perfect building material.

habitat: Forest clearings, edges of moist and dry deciduous forests, open cultivation, orchards, plantations, towns and villages. More associated with wooded habitats than Common Myna.

description.adult_male: Greyish-brown overall with darker head and breast. Distinctive drooping tuft of feathers at the base of the bill. Bill and legs bright yellow, the base of the lower mandible bluish. No bare skin around the eye, unlike Common Myna. Tail blackish with white tips. Iris blue to pale blue-grey in peninsular birds (yellow in northern populations).
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Duller brown, less pronounced bill-base tuft, darker legs, and a brownish iris. Underparts more uniformly brown and softer-toned.
description.in_flight: Shows white tail tips and dark wings; flight strong and somewhat bounding when moving between perches or fields.

behaviour: Highly social and often noisy. Forms large communal roosts in trees, sometimes mixed with other mynas or starlings. Walks confidently on the ground rather than hopping. Often forages in groups in fields and among grazing livestock. Uses a variety of calls – chirps, whistles, chatters – and occasionally mimics other birds. Nests in tree holes, wall crevices and similar cavities.
food: Omnivorous: insects, fruit, grains, kitchen scraps, small invertebrates, flower nectar. Frequently follows ploughing to capture disturbed insects.
did_you_know: The peninsular race, described by Sykes in 1832 from the Deccan, has a blue iris, while Jungle Mynas of northern India look out from yellow eyes.

habitat: Open country, agricultural fields, forest edges, dry grasslands, rocky cliffs, road cuttings, bridges, culverts and buildings – especially where suitable ledges for mud nests exist.

description.adult_male: Glossy blue-black upperparts with a rufous collar and a pale rufous rump. Underparts buff-white with fine dark streaking. Undertail coverts black. Long, deeply forked tail without white spots, unlike Barn Swallow.
description.adult_female: Similar to male with only slightly duller gloss. Plumage pattern and streaking nearly identical.
description.juvenile: Paler and duller with less distinct rufous collar, weaker streaking below and shorter tail streamers.
description.in_flight: Graceful flier with long glides between bursts of quick wingbeats, slower and more buoyant than Barn Swallow. Pale rufous rump and black undertail coverts are striking. Often flies low over fields, water and roads.

behaviour: Highly aerial; spends most of time catching insects on the wing. Calls include soft twittering and chirpy notes. Builds distinctive enclosed mud nests with narrow entrance tubes on vertical surfaces – bridges and culverts commonly used in the Ghats. Migratory populations appear during winter and early summer, often joining mixed swallow flocks.
food: Flying insects: flies, winged termites, beetles, small moths. Feeds low over ground, fields or water.
did_you_know: Its mud nest is a flask with a long tubular entrance tunnel, built under bridges, culverts and rock overhangs; disused nests are readily taken over by House Sparrows and other cavity-nesters.

habitat: Shady forest floor, leaf litter, wet undergrowth, bamboo thickets, coffee plantations, shrubby ravines and riverine forest. Prefers moist wooded areas during wintering.

description.adult_male: Olive-brown above with clean white underparts and two black breast bands, the lower one often broken in the middle. Bold white supercilium. Wings blackish with two broad yellowish-white wingbars. Tail long and blackish with white outer feathers. Distinctive lateral (side-to-side) tail-wagging behaviour.
description.adult_female: Similar to male, sometimes with slightly narrower breast bands but generally identical in field appearance.
description.juvenile: Browner and duller with incomplete or washed-out breast bands. Tail slightly shorter; lateral wagging already present but less pronounced.
description.in_flight: Low, fluttery flight through undergrowth; white outer tail feathers noticeable. Frequently flushes from leaf litter with a sharp call.

behaviour: A solitary winter visitor that walks briskly on the forest floor – rarely seen in open areas. Its lateral tail-wagging is unique among wagtails. Feeds quietly among leaf litter, often in shaded, humid patches. When alarmed, flies up to a low branch before dropping back down. Gives soft 'tsip' calls. Often returns to the same wintering patches year after year.
food: Small insects, ants, beetles, spiders, and other ground-dwelling invertebrates gleaned from leaf litter.
did_you_know: The only member of its genus, it is the one wagtail that swings its tail and rear body from side to side rather than up and down. It breeds in East Asia and winters in peninsular India.

habitat: Dry scrub, open grasslands, fallow fields, rocky plateaus, sparse Acacia scrub, edges of cultivation. Prefers warm, open terrain with scattered bushes.

description.adult_male: Warm brown, heavily streaked above with dark centres to the feathers. Buffy underparts with fine streaking on the breast. Short, rounded tail. Rufous wing panel noticeable when perched and especially in flight. Buff supercilium and strong bill typical of bushlarks.
description.adult_female: Indistinguishable from the male; plumage and wing patches identical.
description.juvenile: Softer brown overall with more diffuse streaking and paler edges to the feathers; less pronounced rufous wing patch; gape pale yellowish.
description.in_flight: Shows rounded wings with rich rufous patches, short tail and weak, fluttery flight. In display the male rises a few metres, then floats down on spread wings and tail, singing.

behaviour: Mostly terrestrial, walking or running quickly between grass clumps. Territorial males perform a short song-flight – rising a few metres with fluttering wings, then parachuting down on outspread wings and tail while singing. Also sings from stones, clods and bush tops. Mostly solitary or in loose pairs.
food: Seeds, grass seeds, ants, beetles, small insects; diet shifts to more insects during breeding season.
did_you_know: Found nowhere outside the Indian subcontinent, it is most easily told from its look-alike bushlarks by the broad rufous wing panel and its song, given from a parachuting display flight.

habitat: Dry and moist deciduous forests, mixed woodland, forest edges, teak plantations, large groves. Prefers tall trees and mid-to-upper canopy.

description.adult_male: Glossy black head, neck, and upper breast contrasting with pale grey back and upperparts. Wings dark with pale edging; underparts white to pale grey. Tail dark with white tips visible in flight.
description.adult_female: Grey-brown above with a pale supercilium; underparts whitish with distinct dark barring on breast and flanks. Lacks the male's black hood.
description.juvenile: Brownish-grey above with faint scaling and mottling; head not fully dark; underparts lightly streaked.
description.in_flight: Slow, slightly undulating flight with white tail edges noticeable. Often moves from tree to tree at mid-canopy height.

behaviour: Frequently solitary or in pairs; sometimes joins mixed-hunting flocks in winter. Methodical canopy forager – gleaning caterpillars and insects from leaves and twigs. Gives soft whistles and harsh notes. Males sit upright when calling. Moves quietly through foliage and is easy to miss unless calling.
food: Caterpillars, beetles, mantises, various insects; occasionally small fruits.
did_you_know: Cuckooshrikes are neither cuckoos nor shrikes: the name refers to their grey, barred plumage. Their closest relatives are the minivets, in the same family Campephagidae.

habitat: Open broadleaf woodland, groves, orchards, riverine forest, gardens, large fruiting trees. Prefers tall, leafy canopy.

description.adult_male: Brilliant golden-yellow plumage, contrasting black eye-stripe and black wings with yellow patches. Bill pinkish-red. Tail black with broad yellow tips and outer edges.
description.adult_female: Greener-olive above, yellowish below with grey or olive streaking on the breast. Eye-stripe weaker. Wings browner.
description.juvenile: Similar to adult female but more streaked below, duller above, and with brownish bill.
description.in_flight: Strong, direct flight with loud flapping; yellow body with contrasting black wings striking against the canopy.

behaviour: Secretive, staying high in leafy canopies. Despite its colour, it often remains hidden. Gives rich fluting whistles – its classic ‘wee-loo’ song carrying far. Moves through branches picking fruit and insects. Sometimes territorial during breeding; nests are cup-shaped slings placed between forked branches.
food: Figs, berries, soft fruits, insects and caterpillars; regularly visits flowering trees for nectar.
did_you_know: Long treated as a race of the Eurasian Golden Oriole, it was recognised as a full species in the 2000s; the black eye-stripe that extends behind the eye is a key difference.

habitat: Dry and moist deciduous forests, open woodland, scrub with tall trees, orchards and wooded gardens; scarcer in wet evergreen forest, where Golden-fronted Leafbird is commoner. Prefers mid-to-upper canopy.

description.adult_male: Brilliant grass-green overall. The face and throat are black, with a dark-blue throat patch inside the black border and a blue moustachial stripe; the black is edged yellow. Wings dark with green edging; tail green with a darker centre.
description.adult_female: Green like the male but lacks the black face and throat; throat turquoise-blue with a blue moustachial stripe. Overall softer appearance.
description.juvenile: Entirely green without mask or blue throat; bill duller and shorter.
description.in_flight: Fast, darting flight across the canopy; green body often blends with foliage.

behaviour: Active and restless canopy forager, hopping among leaves, gleaning insects and nectar. Highly vocal and capable of remarkable mimicry of other birds. Often part of mixed flocks. Territorial males sing rich whistles from mid-canopy positions.
food: Nectar, small insects, caterpillars, berries; frequently visits flowering trees such as Bombax and Erythrina.
did_you_know: Named after Thomas C. Jerdon, the army surgeon whose Birds of India (1862–64) was the first comprehensive account of the subcontinent's birds; Blyth described the species in his honour in 1844.

habitat: Open woodland, gardens, orchards, shrubland, groves, roadside trees. Often in low to mid canopy.

description.adult_male: Bright yellow underparts, greenish back, and black wings with two bold white bars. Breeding males develop black cap, mantle and back, contrasting sharply with yellow underparts.
description.adult_female: Greener overall with olive back and wings; underparts yellowish but paler and more diffuse than male. Wingbars present but less crisp.
description.juvenile: Duller greenish-yellow with less distinct wingbars; underparts washed and unstreaked.
description.in_flight: Flits rapidly through foliage; white wingbars visible in bursts of short flights.

behaviour: Active, acrobatic forager often seen gleaning insects from leaves or hanging upside-down. Frequently in pairs with constant soft contact calls. The breeding male's display is remarkable: it fluffs out its feathers, especially the long white rump plumes, springs into the air and spirals down to a perch like a ball of feathers, then struts with tail fanned. Song a rich, variable series of whistles. Builds neat, cup-shaped nests bound with cobwebs in forked branches.
food: Spiders, caterpillars, beetles, small insects; occasionally small fruit and nectar.
did_you_know: In courtship the male puffs out his long white rump feathers into a ball, leaps upward and parachutes down, a display that gave rise to the old name 'puff-ball bird'.

habitat: Open country, grasslands, paddy fields, sugarcane, village edges, reedbeds, and areas near water. Prefers regions with tall grasses suitable for nest-building.

description.adult_male: In breeding plumage, bright yellow crown and forehead, yellow breast, dark brown streaked upperparts and black mask. Non-breeding males resemble females: buff-brown above, pale below, faint streaking, and no bright yellow.
description.adult_female: Sparrow-like; warm brown above with streaks, pale underparts, faint supercilium, conical bill.
description.juvenile: Buffier and paler than females, with weaker streaking and a yellowish gape. Bill is pale horn-coloured.
description.in_flight: Short, fluttery flight; in breeding males the yellow crown is conspicuous. Gregarious flocks move low over grasslands in bounding flight.

behaviour: A highly colonial species famous for its intricately woven, pendulous nests made of grass strips. Males build multiple 'test' nests and perform display flights to attract females, who inspect and choose preferred nests. Loud, buzzing 'chee-chee' calls around colonies. Feeds in flocks, often mixing with munias and other weavers. Very active and vocal during the monsoon breeding season.
food: Grass seeds, paddy, millet, grain, small insects – especially during breeding.

photos.caption: A Baya Weaver in Bhigwan

did_you_know: Male Baya Weavers are among the few birds that tie true knots, twisting strips of grass or palm into a secure hold that anchors the hanging nest. Breeding is timed to the monsoon.

habitat: Forest edges, bamboo, secondary growth, wooded hillsides, plantations and grassy clearings, often near streams; more a bird of wooded country than the open-field munias.

description.adult_male: Dark chocolate-brown above; underparts white with fine vertical streaking. Bold white rump visible in flight. Black mask and throat patch. Short, thick blue-grey bill typical of munias.
description.adult_female: Plumage identical to male; sexes not separable in the field.
description.juvenile: Warm buff-brown overall, lacking adult streaking. Throat brown, bill pale greyish, rump duller. Often seen begging in post-breeding flocks.
description.in_flight: Tight flocking flight, fast and direct. The bright white rump is striking when birds flush together.

behaviour: Gregarious; moves in compact flocks that shift rapidly between grass patches, bamboo and field edges. Constant soft chipping calls. Frequently clings acrobatically to grass stalks to feed on seeds. Roosts communally and pairs sometimes nest close together in thick vegetation.
food: Grass seeds (primary), paddy grains, small insects (especially during breeding).
did_you_know: The White-rumped Munia is the wild ancestor of the Bengalese or Society Finch, domesticated in East Asia centuries ago and now kept by aviculturists worldwide.

habitat: Forests, wooded hills, forest edges, coffee estates, and open woodland adjoining dense greenery. Often associated with valleys and ridges of the Western Ghats.

description.adult_male: Prominent erect crest; upperparts dark brown; underparts white with heavy brown streaking on breast and belly. Powerful yellow eyes; strong, barred wings; long, banded tail.
description.adult_female: Similar to male but larger and heavier-bodied; otherwise identical plumage.
description.juvenile: Whitish head and body with sparse streaking; crest shorter or absent; underparts buffier; eyes paler.
description.in_flight: Long, broad wings held in a slight dihedral while soaring. Tail well-banded. Appears powerful and slow-flapping, often soaring high over ridges.

behaviour: A dominant forest raptor that soars over canopy edges or perches high to scan for prey. Hunts birds such as junglefowl and pigeons, squirrels, hares, large lizards and snakes. Calls include high, penetrating whistles. Pairs hold large territories. Builds substantial stick nests on large trees.
food: Small to medium-sized mammals, birds, lizards, snakes.
did_you_know: 'Changeable' refers to its variable plumage: crestless races further east occur in pale and dark morphs, whereas the crested race of peninsular India is always pale-bellied.

habitat: Cliffs, escarpments of the Western Ghats, rocky outcrops, coasts, open plains, and occasionally urban high-rises. Prefers exposed ledges for roosting.

description.adult_male: Slate-grey upperparts, finely barred white underparts, bold black hood and moustachial stripe. Yellow cere and eye-ring. Compact, muscular build.
description.adult_female: Similar but much larger and bulkier than male; barring coarser on breast.
description.juvenile: Brown above with buff edges, heavily streaked below instead of barred; facial pattern browner and less sharp.
description.in_flight: Long, pointed wings and long tail. Extremely fast, agile flight. Streamlined silhouette with sickle-shaped wings.

behaviour: Famous for its high-speed stoop, reaching over 300 km/h. Hunts birds in mid-air – doves, pigeons, waders, smaller raptors. Often perches on high cliffs overlooking valleys. Mostly solitary. Wintering individuals remain faithful to seasonal territories. Calls include harsh 'kek-kek-kek' alarms.
food: Primarily birds; occasionally bats.
did_you_know: The Sahyadri breeding birds belong to the Shaheen race (peregrinator), darker above and rufous below; Shaheens nest on the basalt cliffs and often hunt bats and swifts at dusk.

habitat: Open country, grasslands, agricultural fields, forest edges, fallow land, wetlands and lakesides. Often seen hunting over termite swarms and cultivated areas. Prefers open skies and scattered trees or wires for perching.

description.adult_male: Small, slender falcon. Uniform dark slate-grey above and below, with contrasting rufous vent and thighs. Cere, eye-ring and legs orange-red; eyes dark. Tail long and slightly rounded. Wings narrow and pointed.
description.adult_female: Very different from male. Whitish underparts with heavy dark streaking; wings and back brownish with darker centres; pale face with strong dark moustachial stripe; orange-yellow orbital skin. Tail barred. Rufous vent less bright than male.
description.juvenile: Brown upperparts with pale buff edges, strongly streaked below similar to adult female but duller. Facial pattern softer; bill pale. Shows buffy fringes on upperwing coverts.
description.in_flight: Fast, buoyant wingbeats. Long pointed wings reminiscent of hobbies. Often hovers briefly while hunting. Males show striking white underwing coverts against dark flight feathers; females show a barred and spotted underwing. Frequently seen in flocks during migration.

behaviour: Highly migratory; passes through India in huge numbers en route from Mongolia/China to southern Africa. Feeds aerially, often gathering in large flocks over termite emergences. Hunts insects in swift, acrobatic chases. Frequently perches on wires in small flocks. Roosts communally during migration in tall trees or reedbeds. Calls are soft 'kek-kek' notes, but generally silent in wintering grounds.
food: Insects – especially termites, dragonflies, grasshoppers, and beetles. Occasionally takes small vertebrates.
did_you_know: Amur Falcons make the longest sea crossing of any raptor, flying non-stop across the Arabian Sea from India to Africa. Mass hunting in Nagaland was halted in 2013 after local communities turned to protecting the roosts.

habitat: Lakes, marshes, estuaries, rivers, flooded paddy fields and mangroves. Prefers shallow wetlands and edges of standing water.

description.adult_male: Slender all-white egret with long black bill, black legs and bright yellow feet. During breeding displays two long, delicate nape plumes ('aigrettes'), fine breast plumes, and flushed reddish lores.
description.adult_female: Similar to male; sexes indistinguishable in the field. Same white plumage and breeding plumes.
description.juvenile: Duller, lacking head plumes; lores greyish and bill slightly paler. Legs duller with reduced yellow on feet.
description.in_flight: White bird with long trailing black legs and feet; slow, graceful wingbeats. Neck retracted in typical heron posture.

behaviour: Active hunter, often runs, dashes and shuffles its brightly coloured feet to flush prey. Also uses 'stand-and-wait' strategy. Frequently seen alone or in loose groups. Roosts communally with other egrets and herons.
food: Small fish, crustaceans, aquatic insects, frogs, tadpoles.
did_you_know: Its breeding plumes were once so prized by the hat trade that the French word for them, aigrette, gave the egrets their English name; the plume trade drove early bird-protection laws.

habitat: Marshes, ponds, paddy fields, roadside ditches, wet scrub and village tanks. Favours dense vegetation close to water.

description.adult_male: Slate-grey to dark grey body contrasting with pure white face, throat and breast. Rump and vent bright chestnut-red. Legs long, greenish-yellow. Bill yellow with red base.
description.adult_female: Same plumage as male; no reliable differences.
description.juvenile: Browner plumage, dingier face, reduced contrast between grey and white areas. Vent duller.
description.in_flight: Short, weak flight with dangling legs; wings show broad rounded shape and dark-and-white contrast.

behaviour: Bold and noisy. Often emerges from cover, flicking tail rapidly to reveal chestnut vent. Loud, repetitive 'kroo-kroo' calls especially at dusk. Walks confidently on floating vegetation. Territorial pairs year-round.
food: Insects, snails, small fish, worms, seeds and algae.
did_you_know: One of the noisiest birds of the early monsoon, calling in bouts that can last many minutes, day and night. The black, downy chicks leave the nest within hours of hatching.

habitat: Large freshwater wetlands, marshes, paddy fields, village tanks, irrigation reservoirs and flooded grasslands. Strong preference for shallow, snail-rich waterbodies. Also uses seasonal monsoon pools and river-edge mudflats.

description.adult_male: Medium-sized pale grey-white stork with glossy black primaries and secondaries. Bill heavy and yellowish, with a distinct gap between the mandibles when closed – an adaptation for gripping snails. Back and scapulars often appear slightly darker or mottled. In non-breeding plumage, overall greyer with duller bill.
description.adult_female: Indistinguishable from male; sexes are identical in plumage and structure.
description.juvenile: Browner overall with dull greyish-brown plumage, darker legs, and a straighter, duller bill. The characteristic bill gap is less pronounced or absent in early juvenile stages and becomes clearer with age.
description.in_flight: Steady, powerful wingbeats followed by glides. Shows contrasting black flight feathers and broad pale upperwings. Neck and legs fully extended, typical of storks. Bill appears long and downcurved in profile.

behaviour: Feeds by probing mud and shallow water for snails, manipulating them efficiently using the specialised open-bill mechanism. Often forages in loose groups, especially in snail-rich wetlands. Frequently seen soaring high on thermals when commuting between feeding and roosting sites. Roosts colonially in tall trees, often alongside other waterbirds such as ibis and herons. Calls rarely, mostly a quiet bill-clattering at nests.
food: Aquatic snails (particularly Pila species), freshwater molluscs, frogs, small fish, large insects and aquatic invertebrates.

photos.caption: Asian Openbill showing its characteristic bill gap. Bhigwan, Maharashtra.

did_you_know: Juveniles hatch with normal closed bills: the signature 'open bill' develops later for snail feeding.

habitat: Shallow ponds, lakes, marshes, paddy fields and irrigation canals; prefers still or slow-moving water with vegetation.

description.adult_male: Warm rufous-brown body, darker crown, long neck and grey face. Chestnut lesser wing coverts and rump. Eyes dark, ringed with a conspicuous yellow to orange eye-ring.
description.adult_female: Similar to male, sexes identical in field.
description.juvenile: Duller brown with less contrast on wings; underparts buffier.
description.in_flight: Shows rounded wings and warm rufous body; calls a soft, descending whistling note while flying.

behaviour: Often seen in tight flocks. Diurnal loafers and nocturnal feeders. Frequently perches on branches over water. Very tolerant of human presence and commonly seen in village tanks.
food: Aquatic vegetation, seeds, rice grains, small molluscs and aquatic insects.
did_you_know: Unlike most ducks it often nests well above the ground, in tree hollows or the old nests of kites and crows, and the ducklings jump down soon after hatching.

habitat: Large rivers, reservoirs, lakes, estuaries and coastal wetlands. Prefers deeper inland waters than Little Cormorant.

description.adult_male: Slim dark cormorant with long narrow bill and sharp hook. Striking blue-green eye. Breeding plumage shows a small white tuft behind the eye; non-breeding birds have yellowish facial skin and a paler throat. Head and neck appear more elongated than Little Cormorant.
description.adult_female: Similar to male; sexes identical.
description.juvenile: Browner and duller with paler throat; lacks breeding streaking.
description.in_flight: Fast and direct flight with powerful wingbeats; long neck stretched out. Flies in loose lines over water.

behaviour: Dives gracefully and swims low in water with only head and neck visible. Often perches on snags, spreading wings to dry. Breeds colonially with other waterbirds.
food: Fish primarily; occasionally aquatic insects and crustaceans.
did_you_know: Indian Cormorants fish cooperatively: flocks form a broad line across the water and drive fish ahead of them before diving together.

habitat: Small ponds, village tanks, marshes, irrigation canals and ditches with abundant emergent vegetation.

description.adult_male: Small, rounded waterbird with very short tail (often invisible). Breeding plumage features rich rufous neck and cheeks, dark brown body, contrasting pale gape patch. Bill short and dark.
description.adult_female: Like male; sexes are not separable in the field. Same rufous neck during breeding season.
description.juvenile: Brownish overall with pale stripes on face and neck. Duller and less rufous than adults.
description.in_flight: Very rarely seen flying; weak fluttering flight with trailing legs. Usually avoids flight by diving.

behaviour: Extremely aquatic, seldom comes ashore. Dives instantly when disturbed and may stay submerged for long periods. Eats its own feathers and feeds feathers to chicks – an adaptation to protect the stomach from fish bones. Builds floating nests in reeds. Quiet but gives sharp, trilling calls during breeding.
food: Aquatic insects, larvae, small fish, tadpoles and crustaceans.
did_you_know: Stripe-headed chicks ride on their parents' backs for their first weeks, and an adult leaving the nest covers the eggs with weed to hide them.

habitat: Rocky streams, riverbanks, lakeshores, reservoirs, mangroves and small forest streams.

description.adult_male: Brownish-grey above with fine streaking; white below with characteristic upcurving breast patches. Distinctive teetering (bobbing) motion while walking.
description.adult_female: Very similar; sexes not distinguishable in field.
description.juvenile: Fresher-edged wing feathers, buffy fringes, less crisp patterning; retains teetering habit.
description.in_flight: Shows a sharp white wingbar and dark upperparts; flies low over water with rapid, shallow wingbeats.

behaviour: Usually solitary and highly active along water edges. Constant tail/body bobbing while foraging is diagnostic. Often flushes with a sharp 'twee-wee-wee' call. Winters widely across peninsular India.
food: Aquatic insects, crustaceans, worms and small molluscs.
did_you_know: Its flight is as distinctive as its bobbing walk: it skims low over water on stiff, bowed wings with flickering, shallow beats, quite unlike other small waders.

habitat: Open fields, dry riverbeds, cultivation, grasslands and edges of waterbodies. Frequently near villages.

description.adult_male: Black crown, face, throat and chest; white belly and flanks; brown wings and back. Bright red wattle in front of eye, red bill with black tip, and long yellow legs.
description.adult_female: Same as male; no difference in plumage.
description.juvenile: Browner with duller face pattern and buff-edged feathers. Wattles reduced or absent.
description.in_flight: Shows bold black-and-white wings; loud calls while flying. Strong, straight flight.

behaviour: Extremely vocal and alert. Famous call resembles 'Did-he-do-it?' or 'Tit-tit-dit!'. Ground nester; bravely defends nesting area with distraction displays – feigning injury to lure predators away. Often active at night around wetlands.
food: Insects, beetles, ants, earthworms and small invertebrates.
did_you_know: Nesting on bare ground in the hot season, adults soak their belly feathers in water and return to wet and cool the eggs.

habitat: Scrub, dense undergrowth, forest edges, agricultural fields, bamboo groves and gardens. Often near human habitation.

description.adult_male: Large cuckoo with glossy black head/body, rich chestnut wings and very long black tail. Eyes deep ruby-red. Heavy, arched bill.
description.adult_female: Same overall appearance; females sometimes slightly browner.
description.juvenile: Browner body with buff barring on wings and tail; duller eye colour.
description.in_flight: Heavy, floppy flight with broad wings; chestnut wings show clearly when flying short distances.

behaviour: Solitary, slow-moving and skulking. Gives deep, booming 'coop-coop-coop' or 'hoop-hoop' calls – often at dawn and during monsoon. Poor flier; prefers running and clambering through vegetation. Known to take nestlings of other birds.
food: Large insects, caterpillars, snails, small reptiles, frogs, bird eggs and nestlings.
did_you_know: Unlike most cuckoos it is not a brood parasite: pairs build their own domed nest of twigs and leaves in dense cover and raise the young themselves.

habitat: Extremely adaptable: wetlands, paddy fields, village tanks, mangroves, garden ponds, forest edges, plantations, dry scrub, grassland, roadside wires and even urban areas. Unusual among kingfishers in frequently occurring far from water.

description.adult_male: Large, colourful kingfisher with rich chestnut-brown head, neck and underparts; bright turquoise-blue wings, scapulars and back; clean white throat and breast forming a clear contrast. Bill long, heavy and orange-red; legs bright red. Iris dark brown.
description.adult_female: Plumage identical to male; sexes cannot be separated reliably in the field.
description.juvenile: Duller overall with browner-edged blue wing feathers, paler and more brownish bill, and slightly less contrasting throat patch. Underparts washed buff.
description.in_flight: Strong, direct, fast flight with rapid wingbeats. Blue upperwings flash intensely; large red bill and white breast panel are visible even at distance.

behaviour: Bold, vocal and conspicuous. Hunts from exposed perches such as wires, poles, treetops or fence posts. Takes prey with quick dives, short sallies or ground strikes. Regularly hawks insects on the wing. Gives loud, rattling 'kek-kek-kek-kek' calls, especially at dawn and after rain. Highly territorial and often aggressive toward other kingfishers. Frequently perches motionless for long periods before launching sudden attacks.
food: Wide-ranging diet: fish, frogs, tadpoles, large insects (grasshoppers, dragonflies, beetles), lizards, small snakes, and occasionally rodents or small birds.

photos.caption: Adult perched near a stream flowing in the Sinhagad valley.

did_you_know: It often lives far from water, hunting lizards, insects, and even small rodents.

habitat: Evergreen, semi-evergreen, and moist deciduous forests of the Western Ghats; prefers tall forest with fruiting trees, especially figs.

description.adult_male: Large grey hornbill with a long tail; pale grey head with a broad whitish supercilium and fine white streaks; grey-brown upperparts, paler below with rufous-tinged vent. Long curved bill with no casque: in the male orange-yellow with a darker reddish base and pale yellow tip. Tail blackish with white tips to the outer feathers.
description.adult_female: Similar to male but bill plain yellow with a black patch at the base of the lower mandible and a black line along the culmen. Head streaking identical.
description.juvenile: Duller grey overall with a whitish iris; bill smaller and pale horn-coloured. Lacks crisp head streaking.
description.in_flight: Strong, steady wingbeats; wings appear broad and rounded. Tail long and dark with pale tip visible in good light.

behaviour: Highly arboreal and strongly frugivorous, moving in small groups through mid- to upper canopy. Loud, cackling calls echo through forests at dawn and dusk. Nests in tree cavities; the female seals herself inside with her droppings, leaving only a slit through which the male passes food. Plays a key ecological role as a seed disperser of large forest fruits. Populations are declining due to habitat fragmentation across the Western Ghats.
food: Primarily figs and other large fruits; also insects, small reptiles and occasional small vertebrates.
did_you_know: Among the smallest of Asia's hornbills, it is the only Indian hornbill without a casque. The nesting female stays walled into her cavity for several weeks, fed through a slit by her mate.

habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous forests, wooded valleys, orchards, plantations and well-treed cultivation; also visits fruiting trees in villages.

description.adult_male: Striking parakeet with plum-coloured head, red on the forehead shading to purple-blue on the nape and cheeks, narrow black chin stripe and black neck ring. Green body with a small maroon shoulder patch and bluish-green tail tipped white. Upper mandible orange-yellow, lower dark.
description.adult_female: Head blue-grey with a yellow collar; no black chin stripe, neck ring or maroon shoulder patch. Upper mandible pale yellow. Body green with similar tail.
description.juvenile: Both sexes green-headed with only a hint of bluish wash; no neck ring; bill pale horn-coloured.
description.in_flight: Fast, direct flight with rapid wingbeats; long tail streamers and blue rump stand out.

behaviour: Noisy, fast-moving flocks, often at canopy height. Frequently mixes with other parakeets at fruiting trees. Calls include sharp 'twit-twit' notes and rolling chatter. Told from the Malabar Parakeet by its plum-coloured (male) or grey (female) head and the absence of the Malabar’s blue-green body.
food: Fruits, seeds, berries, leaf buds, nectar; raids crops occasionally.
did_you_know: Found only in the Indian subcontinent, it takes about a year for young birds to exchange their all-green heads for the plum of the male or the grey of the female.

habitat: Dry and moist deciduous forest edges, scrub-jungle, farmland, riverine belts and village outskirts. Avoids deep forest interior.

description.adult_male: Magnificent iridescent blue neck and breast; long shimmering train of elongated uppertail coverts with 'eye' patterns. Crest fan-shaped. Wings barred black and white with chestnut primaries. Train length highly variable.
description.adult_female: Brown and white, lacking train. Greenish sheen on neck; crest smaller and brownish. Overall slimmer and smaller.
description.juvenile: Duller brown; young males begin showing metallic neck sheen early but lack train.
description.in_flight: Heavy, powerful flight; broad, rounded wings; train trails behind and is not aerodynamic, so males avoid long flights.

behaviour: Ground-feeding omnivore, often near water and cultivation. Males display extravagant train-fanning ('courtship fan') mainly during monsoon breeding. Loud 'kee-ow' calls echo at dawn and dusk. Roosts on tall trees. Generally tolerant of human presence.
food: Seeds, grain, insects, small snakes, lizards, and berries.
did_you_know: Declared India's national bird in 1963 and given the highest legal protection under the Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972.

habitat: Dense moist deciduous and evergreen forests with large trees; favours ravines, steep slopes and secluded valleys.

description.adult_male: Massive owl with prominent ear tufts, dark brown upperparts, bold black spotting on pale underparts, and large dark-brown eyes. Broad, powerful head and deep hoot.
description.adult_female: Slightly larger than male but similar in plumage; sexes not easily distinguished.
description.juvenile: Fluffier white to creamy plumage with incomplete spotting; developing ear tufts.
description.in_flight: Large, broad-winged silhouette; slow, deep wingbeats; silent flight typical of owls.

behaviour: Solitary, strictly nocturnal predator. Roosts in dense foliage or shaded rock ledges during the day. Deep, booming calls carry long distances. Takes surprisingly large prey, including junglefowl, hares, large rodents and other birds. Rare and easily overlooked in dense forest.
food: Large rodents, hares, junglefowl, pigeons, small mammals and occasionally reptiles.
did_you_know: In Sri Lanka it is widely held to be the 'ulama' or devil bird, whose eerie, scream-like night call has been the stuff of legend in literature since the nineteenth century.

habitat: Open country near large waterbodies, estuaries, river banks, wetlands, and paddy fields. Unlike the Green Bee-eater, it is strongly associated with water and rarely found in dry scrub far from aquatic sources.

description.adult_male: Larger and sleeker than the Green Bee-eater. Upperparts are green with a distinct golden-bronze sheen. Face has a bold black mask bordered by fine blue lines above and below. Throat is rich chestnut-rufous, shading into a yellowish-green breast. Rump and tail are bright azure-blue. Central tail feathers are elongated into narrow 'pins' (streamers).
description.adult_female: Visually similar to the male with identical plumage patterns; however, the central tail streamers are often shorter or sometimes absent depending on the moult stage.
description.juvenile: Much duller than adults. The throat is pale fading to whitish-buff (lacking the rich chestnut). The plumage lacks the bronze sheen, appearing flatter green. Central tail streamers are absent, and the breast often shows faint scaly mottling.
description.in_flight: Flight is graceful, buoyant, and agile, often involving long glides on flat triangular wings. The bright blue rump and tail contrast sharply with the green back, which is a key identification feature in flight. Gives a distinctive, rolling liquid call 'te-lew' or 'pruu-pruu' while flying.

behaviour: Highly gregarious. Perches on wires, exposed branches, or reeds near water, sallying out to snatch dragonflies and bees in mid-air. Returns to the perch to batter the prey against the branch to remove stingers before swallowing. Roosts communally in huge numbers (sometimes thousands) in mangroves, coconut groves, or tall trees near water, creating a deafening spectacle at dusk.
food: Specialises in dragonflies, bees, and wasps; also takes butterflies and flying ants.
did_you_know: They nest in colonies by excavating tunnels into sandy riverbanks or flat open ground, sometimes digging burrows nearly 2 metres long.

habitat: Open agricultural fields, grasslands, forest edges, scrubland, village outskirts and along roadsides. Prefers open habitats with scattered perches such as wires, poles or bare trees.

description.adult_male: Striking combination of vivid blues and warm browns. Crown and nape pale turquoise-blue; mantle and breast warm rufous-brown; throat lilac-washed. Wings extremely bright with deep ultramarine, turquoise and purple-blue panels. Rump bright blue; tail short with bluish tip. Bill strong and dark; eyes pale brown.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike, with identical colouration and pattern; females may be marginally duller but not reliably distinguishable in the field.
description.juvenile: Duller overall with browner upperparts and less saturated blues. Underparts buffy and plain; wing panels lack full brilliance of adults. Throat and breast less lilac-toned; flight feathers narrower and less contrasting.
description.in_flight: Highly distinctive flashing bands of blue and purple on the wings. Underwing shows three contrasting bars: deep blue, pale blue and purple. Flight strong and purposeful, alternating with sudden swoops. During display the bird performs exaggerated rolls, dives and loops, revealing the bright turquoise patches.

behaviour: Typically seen perched conspicuously on wires, poles or bare branches, scanning the ground for prey. Hunts by dropping from a perch in a rapid glide to seize insects or small vertebrates. Frequently active near roadsides where insects are abundant. During the breeding season performs its famous 'rolling' aerial display with tumbling, diving loops accompanied by harsh calls. Territorial and vocal; emits repeated rasping 'chack-chack' notes while displaying.
food: Large insects such as grasshoppers, crickets and beetles; also feeds on small reptiles, frogs, large termites and occasionally small rodents.

photos.caption: Adult perched on roadside wire showing typical bright turquoise crown and rufous breast.
Individual with vivid ultramarine and purple wing panels.

did_you_know: During the breeding season, Indian Rollers perform spectacular aerial displays – barrel rolls, steep dives and sudden flips – which is where the name 'roller' comes from.

habitat: Deciduous and evergreen forests, bamboo clumps. Prefers areas with large arboreal ant nests, especially in mid-storey trees.

description.adult_male: Unmistakable rufous-brown plumage with black barring on the flanks and wings. Male has a small red cheek patch.
description.adult_female: Unmistakable rufous-brown plumage with black barring on the flanks and wings; lacks the male’s red cheek patch.
description.juvenile: Duller, paler rufous overall with less distinct barring; the male’s red cheek patch is absent or replaced by dark mottling. Feathers may appear looser and fluffier.
description.in_flight: Typical woodpecker flight: strong, undulating and direct, but rather rapid. The rufous body and heavily barred wings are conspicuous against the black underwings.

behaviour: Forages mainly on ant-ridden trees. Unique among woodpeckers in its near-obligate association with arboreal ant nests of Crematogaster (Pagoda ants). Pairs excavate nest chambers inside active ant nests – tolerating the ants’ aggressive defence. Often clambers in dense tangles and bamboo. Calls are fast, high-pitched and sharp.
food: Arboreal ants, termites, larvae and other small invertebrates. Shows a strong preference for Crematogaster ants and their brood.

photos.caption: The male of the species: with the small red cheek patch. Dandeli, Karnataka.

did_you_know: It excavates its nest chamber inside the living carton nests of Crematogaster ants, which defend their colony fiercely against most intruders but tolerate the woodpecker and its chicks.

habitat: Moist deciduous, semi-evergreen and evergreen forests of the Western Ghats; also wooded gardens, orchards, and well-treed plantations with abundant fruiting figs. Endemic to peninsular India: commonest in the Western Ghats but also in the Eastern Ghats and an outlying Satpura population.

description.adult_male: Green-bodied barbet with brown crown and cheek, clean white cheek patch, and fine white streaks on throat and upper breast. Bill stout and pale horn-coloured. Eye-ring dull bluish.
description.adult_female: Similar to the male; sexes extremely difficult to separate in the field.
description.juvenile: Duller overall with browner head and less distinct white streaking; cheek patch muted or washed greyish. Bill darker and plumage less crisp.
description.in_flight: Fast, direct flight between fruiting trees; wings short and rounded. Appears as a compact green bird flashing through the canopy.

behaviour: Arboreal, remaining high in canopy or mid-storey. Often detected by its persistent, resonant 'kutrook… kutrook…' calls delivered from concealed perches. Feeds by hopping methodically through foliage, taking fruits and figs, occasionally hawking insects. Frequently associates with other frugivores at fig trees.
food: Figs, other forest fruits, berries, flowers, and occasional insects.

photos.caption: A white-cheeked barbet with its distinctive white cheek patch below the eye, spotted near Bengaluru.

did_you_know: Its monotonous, metronomic call can run unbroken for minutes at a time and is one of the most constant sounds of the Ghats forests.

habitat: Grasslands, scrub, cultivation (often hides in dense cover).

description.adult_male: Small, quail-like bird with yellow legs and bill; mottled rufous and black upperparts, buff underparts with dark spotting on the breast sides. The duller and smaller sex.
description.adult_female: Larger and brighter than the male, with a rich rufous hindneck and collar; as in all buttonquails the female courts and the male incubates.
description.juvenile: Duller, paler brown overall with less distinct rufous and black mottling. The breast and flanks are washed with dull buff and streaks are more blurred.
description.in_flight: Short, rapid burst of flight before dropping into cover; wings are short and rounded, with the bird appearing weak-winged and fast. It flies low over the grass and rarely for long distances.

behaviour: Terrestrial, runs quickly to escape rather than flushing; the female is polyandrous (mates with multiple males) and uses a low, soft booming call to attract mates. They rely heavily on camouflage in dense grass clumps.
food: Seeds and insects.
did_you_know: Buttonquails are quails in name only: they are relatives of the waders in the order Charadriiformes, and the roles are reversed, with the larger, brighter female courting and the male incubating.

habitat: Montane evergreen forests (sholas), adjoining moist grass–forest mosaics, and heavily wooded ravines; typically above 900–1000 m, locally down to 700 m in wetter zones.

description.adult_male: Deep slaty-blue overall with a velvety appearance; slightly brighter blue on the forehead, face and rump. Wings and tail darker with bluish edges. A small but distinctive white patch at the base of the outer tail feathers is visible when flicked or in flight. Eyes dark and prominent.
description.adult_female: Duller, more grey-washed blue than the male, particularly on the head and upperparts. The white basal tail patch is present but less contrasting. Underparts are slightly paler and more greyish.
description.juvenile: Dark brownish overall with buff spotting and scaling on the head, mantle, and breast. Wings show faint pale edgings. Tail patch barely visible or only hinted. Transition to blue begins on the scapulars and rump.
description.in_flight: Short, direct, low flight between perches. The flicked tail often reveals the diagnostic white basal patch. Overall a compact, rounded-wing profile.

behaviour: A quiet, unobtrusive shola specialist. Typically perches upright on low to mid-level branches inside dense, moist forest, making short sallies to capture insects. Frequently flicks the tail when alert. Often forages singly or in loose association with mixed-species flocks. Outside the breeding season it becomes notably silent and inconspicuous, relying heavily on sit-and-wait hunting from shaded perches.
food: Primarily insects – caught by short aerial sallies or gleaned from foliage. Occasionally takes small arthropods from the understorey leaves, mossy trunks, and lichen-covered branches.
did_you_know: One of the few Western Ghats endemics confined almost entirely to the high sholas; below about 900 m it is quickly replaced by the Tickell’s Blue Flycatcher.

habitat: High-elevation shola forests, dense undergrowth, forest-floor thickets, leaf-litter tangles, forest edges, and streamside vegetation above 1200–1400 m.

description.adult_male: Compact flycatcher with rich, deep orange underparts and rump contrasting strongly with a glossy black head, mantle, wings and tail. Wings show subtle orange edgings. Iris dark, bill fine and black. Unmistakable.
description.adult_female: Black of the male replaced by dark brown on head, wings and tail; orange underparts and mantle duller. A pale eye-ring is noticeable. Pattern still unmistakable but less contrasting overall.
description.juvenile: Brownish overall with heavy buff spotting and scaling on head, mantle and breast. Wings and tail show faint rufous edges. No sharp black–orange contrast.
description.in_flight: Low, quick, fluttering flight through dense vegetation. Short, rounded wings give a bouncy, weak-looking flight; orange rump flashes briefly.

behaviour: A shola undergrowth specialist that keeps close to the ground. Skulks in dense vegetation, hopping rapidly between low perches and leaf litter. Frequently pumps or flicks its tail. Often seen foraging singly or in pairs, rarely joining mixed flocks. Breeding birds give sharp ticks and soft trills; otherwise quiet. Territorial during the breeding season.
food: Small insects and other invertebrates gleaned from leaf litter, mossy logs, low shrubs, and ground-level foliage.
did_you_know: Long placed in its own genus Ochromela because of its odd colours, DNA studies have shown it is a true Ficedula flycatcher that evolved in isolation in the high sholas.

habitat: Moist evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, well-wooded valleys, plantations with tall trees and fruit-rich areas dominated by figs, mainly in the lowlands and foothills below about 1200 m.

description.adult_male: Small, plump green barbet with a crimson forehead, crown and throat. Sides of the face and throat blue, bordered below by a thin blackish line; orbital skin orange-red. Rest of body grass-green, paler below; bill dark.
description.adult_female: Similar to male; sexes very alike with only minor variation in brightness.
description.juvenile: Duller, with little or no red on the head and throat and a weaker blue face pattern; orbital skin pale.
description.in_flight: Direct, shallow-beating flight with fast wingbeats; flashes of green body and dark wings. Usually moves short distances between fruiting trees.

behaviour: Arboreal and often sedentary around fruiting figs. Gives a fast, rolling 'pukuruk-pukuruk' from high canopy perches, noticeably quicker than the measured 'tonk' of the Coppersmith Barbet. Excavates nest holes in softwood trees and dead branches. Often joins bulbuls and other barbets at fruiting trees.
food: Figs and other fruits; supplements diet with insects, especially when feeding chicks.
did_you_know: Long treated as a race of Sri Lanka's Crimson-fronted Barbet, it is now recognised as a Western Ghats endemic; its hurried, rattling call is the easiest way to tell it from the Coppersmith Barbet it so often shares a fig tree with.

habitat: Wet evergreen forests, shola edges, wooded plantations, forest gardens, and groves with berry-rich shrubs and figs across mid-to-high elevations.

description.adult_male: Tiny and compact, plain olive-grey above and dull whitish below with a faint yellowish wash and an indistinct pale supercilium. Bill short, slender and slightly decurved. Lacks any bright colour. Iris dark; legs dark slate.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Duller, washed-out grey-brown overall with softer contrast; underparts more uniformly buff.
description.in_flight: Fast, tiny, whirring flight with short bursts between fruiting bushes and canopy clusters.

behaviour: Highly active and restless, constantly moving between berries and flowers. Frequently hovers briefly to pick fruit or probe blossoms. A key disperser of mistletoe (Loranthaceae) seeds. Gives thin, high-pitched tsee or tsi notes, often from the canopy.
food: Berries, small fruits, nectar, and occasional spiders or small arthropods.
did_you_know: It is a mistletoe specialist: the sticky seeds pass through its gut in minutes and the bird wipes them off onto a branch, planting the parasite exactly where it needs to grow.

habitat: High-altitude shola forests north of the Palghat Gap (Nilgiris, Wayanad, Brahmagiris, Bababudan Hills), keeping to dark, dense undergrowth above about 1200 m.

description.adult_male: Chunky robin-flycatcher with long pinkish legs and short tail. Dark slaty-blue head, mantle, throat, and breast. Flanks and belly warm rufous, often turning buffy or whitish at centre. Black lores; faint bluish brow.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Brownish with heavy scaling on breast and mantle; blue adult tones appear gradually.
description.in_flight: Short-tailed, round-winged, low flight across forest floor; often drops quickly back into cover.

behaviour: A skulker of dark, damp shola interiors. Hunts insects on the forest floor or low branches, hopping rapidly with long-legged gait. Frequently gives sharp tit-like notes and harsh rattles; song is a mix of thin whistles and twanging buzzes. Can be surprisingly confiding when encountered but rarely leaves deep cover. Very site-faithful.
food: Insects and small invertebrates gathered from leaf litter, moss, and low vegetation.
did_you_know: For over a century it was called a shortwing and placed with Brachypteryx; DNA work in 2017 showed it is an old, isolated lineage of flycatcher, and the new genus Sholicola was coined from 'shola' and the Latin for dweller.

habitat: Dense, wet undergrowth and edges of high-altitude shola forests south of the Palghat Gap (Anamalais, Palnis, Cardamom Hills and Agasthyamalai).

description.adult_male: Dark slaty-blue upperparts, throat and breast with black lores. Belly and vent clean white, contrasting with bluish-grey flanks. Lacks the pale brow of the Nilgiri Blue Robin. Bill black; legs pinkish-brown.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Brown with scaly spotting and streaks; blue tones develop with age.
description.in_flight: Low, direct movement across dense vegetation, often just above the forest floor; white belly flashes briefly.

behaviour: Exceptionally secretive. Forages very low – often on or just above the forest floor – taking insects from leaf litter and tangled undergrowth. More often heard than seen; song is a clear, melodious series of whistles used in territory defence. Shy and quick to retreat into thickets.
food: Insects, small invertebrates, and other arthropods from damp forest-floor microhabitats.
did_you_know: The Palghat Gap, a 30 km break in the Ghats, separates it from its sister species the Nilgiri Sholakili; the two have been isolated for millions of years on opposite sides of this gap.

habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous forests, especially areas with fruiting trees.

description.adult_male: Olive-green with a grey forehead and crown, a maroon mantle and wing coverts, yellow wing-bars and yellowish-green underparts. Feet red.
description.adult_female: Duller; lacks the maroon mantle, which is olive-green like the back.
description.juvenile: Like the female but duller.
description.in_flight: Fast, direct flight; yellow feet visible.

behaviour: Arboreal and social, feeding in flocks high in the canopy on fruit, where its green plumage makes it remarkably hard to see. Gives a mellow, modulated, whistling song from the treetops.
food: Fruits and berries, especially figs.
did_you_know: It was split in 2014 from the Pompadour Green Pigeon complex, which once stretched from India to the Philippines; the Western Ghats population is the only one with a grey forehead.

habitat: Mature moist deciduous and evergreen forests with tall, old trees. It is highly dependent on large, dying timber for nesting and foraging. Also seen in old plantations (coffee/cardamom) that retain massive shade trees.

description.adult_male: The largest woodpecker in peninsular India. Glossy slate-black upperparts, throat, and breast, contrasting sharply with a clean white belly and white rump. Features a spectacular bright red crest covering the entire crown and a distinct red malar (moustache) stripe. Eyes are creamy-yellow.
description.adult_female: Similar in size and plumage to the male, but the red is restricted to the nape (back of the head). The forecrown and malar area are black, lacking the moustache stripe.
description.juvenile: Softer, sooty-black plumage rather than glossy. The crest is shorter and duller red. Throat often shows faint greyish or whitish streaking. Eyes are dark brown, lightening with age.
description.in_flight: Flight is distinctively different from other woodpeckers: heavy, direct, and 'crow-like' with slow, deep wingbeats, rather than the bounding (undulating) flight of smaller species. The brilliant white rump and white underwing linings flash conspicuously against the black wings.

behaviour: Shy and wary, often retreating to the far side of a trunk when observed. Its presence is usually announced by a loud, ringing, single-note call 'kyuk' or a manic, laughing trill. Drums loudly and powerfully on resonant dead wood. Forages by scaling off large plates of bark to expose borers, often leaving piles of debris at the base of trees.
food: Large wood-boring beetle larvae, ants (especially large Camponotus carpenter ants), termites, and other insects extracted from decaying heartwood.
did_you_know: It has a specialised 'chisel-tipped' bill and shock-absorbent skull that allow it to hammer into hard hardwoods that smaller woodpeckers cannot penetrate.

habitat: Dense, shaded understorey of evergreen and moist deciduous forests, especially in ravines, stream valleys, and mature forest interiors from low to mid-elevations (300–1500 m).

description.adult_male: Striking. Black head and upper breast with pale blue orbital skin and a bluish bill; narrow white breast band separating the crimson belly and undertail coverts. Back and rump cinnamon-brown; wings finely vermiculated black-and-white. Long tail chestnut above with white outer feathers below.
description.adult_female: Head and breast olive-brown instead of black; belly and undertail orange-buff. Back and rump brown; wings barred brown and buff. Tail brown above with white outer feathers.
description.juvenile: Resembles the female but duller, with less distinct wing barring.
description.in_flight: Slow, buoyant, dipping flight with deep, deliberate wingbeats. The long, chestnut upper tail and white-tipped underside flash as it moves between shaded perches.

behaviour: A classic sit-and-wait forest insectivore. Perches motionless for long intervals on horizontal branches in dark ravines, swivelling its head quietly before sallying to snap insects, spiders, and sometimes small lizards. Prefers twilight-rich microhabitats and shady gullies. Pairs often stay in loose contact with soft, repeated notes. Highly sensitive to disturbance and easily overlooked despite bright colours.
food: Insects, spiders and caterpillars; occasionally small lizards and berries.
did_you_know: Trogons are the only birds with heterodactyl feet, the first and second toes pointing backwards. Sitting quietly for long spells, this is the sole trogon of the Western Ghats and is far more often heard than seen.

habitat: Thick undergrowth, dry and moist deciduous forests, scrub, and bamboo groves. In the Sahyadris, it is often found in shady ravines, coffee plantations, and damp nullahs during migration.

description.adult_male: A stubby, tailless bird famous as the 'Navrang' (Nine Colours). Features a bold black stripe through the eye, a white throat, and a buff crown with a central black stripe. Upperparts are emerald green with a shining cobalt-blue shoulder patch. Underparts are warm buff, transitioning to a vivid crimson vent and undertail coverts.
description.adult_female: Identical to the male in plumage; sexes cannot be distinguished in the field.
description.juvenile: Significantly duller. The crown is plain brown without the distinct black stripe; upperparts are olive-brown rather than green; the red vent is washed out or pinkish.
description.in_flight: Transforms from a ground-bird into a flash of colour. It shows large, rounded wings with a striking white patch (primary coverts) that contrasts brilliantly with the black and blue wings. The tiny tail is barely visible.

behaviour: Strictly terrestrial during the day, hopping on long pink legs to turn over dead leaves for prey. It has a distinct 'stop-start' motion, often flicking its short tail. In the northern Sahyadris it arrives with the monsoon to breed, and from June to August its two-note whistle rings through the hill forests at dawn and dusk; in the far south it is mainly a silent winter visitor. Roosts high in trees at night, unusual for a ground feeder.
food: Earthworms, termites, ants, beetles, and snails. It often uses a stone as an 'anvil' to crack open snail shells.
did_you_know: Its Hindi name 'Navrang' means 'Nine Colours,' referring to the green, blue, black, white, buff, ochre, brown, pink, and red in its plumage.

habitat: Restricted to the Western Ghats (from Goa southwards). Prefers dense evergreen forests, shola edges, and swampy areas dominated by Ochlandra reeds (bamboo). Rarely comes out into open clearings.

description.adult_male: Distinctive separation of colours: a clean, slate-grey head and throat that contrasts sharply with an olive-green back and wings. The rump is brighter yellow-green. Underparts are yellowish. A key field mark is the pale white or bluish-white iris, which gives it a 'staring' expression, unlike the dark eyes of most bulbuls. Bill is greenish-grey.
description.adult_female: Similar to male but often slightly duller; the head may appear a darker, sootier grey rather than slate.
description.juvenile: Head is olive-brown (not grey); the iris is dark (not pale). The distinct contrast between head and body is missing.
description.in_flight: Flight is weak and dipping; usually seen making short dashes across gaps in the canopy. The tail appears squared-off and greyish at the tip.

behaviour: Much shyer than the Red-vented or Red-whiskered Bulbuls. It tends to forage in the mid-story to upper canopy, often solitary or in pairs. Its call is unique: a sharp, metallic single note 'chwang' or 'pink', and a fast, bubbling chatter. It plays a vital role in dispersing seeds of forest vines and figs.
food: Frugivorous, feeding on small berries (Lantana, Ficus) and fruits; occasionally takes insects during the breeding season.

photos.caption: A grey-headed bulbul perched at Udupi, Karnataka.
