description.adult_female: Similar to Eurasian Kestrel female but generally smaller, paler and more lightly barred; separation often difficult in the field.
description.juvenile: Resembles female; brown above with darker barring and streaked underparts, but overall paler and more delicate-looking than Eurasian Kestrel.
description.in_flight: Pointed wings and long tail like other kestrels, but tends to hover less frequently than Eurasian Kestrel, relying more on low glides and short flapping flights over fields. Structure slightly smaller and daintier.

behaviour: Highly gregarious in winter across its core range, often forming large communal roosts and feeding flocks. Where it occurs in India, typically hunts over open farmland, focusing heavily on insect swarms.
food: Insects (mainly grasshoppers, beetles and other large invertebrates), and occasionally small vertebrates.
did_you_know: A close view reveals whitish claws, unlike the black claws of the Common Kestrel. Once listed as Vulnerable, it was downgraded to Least Concern in 2011 after surveys showed its populations were far larger and more stable than feared.

habitat: Gardens, groves, scrub, thin forest, and tree-covered urban areas.

description.adult_male: Tiny, bright yellow-green bird with a prominent, distinct white ring of feathers around the eye. Yellow throat, pale greyish-white belly.
description.adult_female: Similar to male; sexes look alike.
description.juvenile: Duller plumage overall, with less vivid yellow-green and a less distinct eye-ring.
description.in_flight: Small, rapid, flitting flight; often flies in tight, cohesive flocks moving between tree crowns.

behaviour: Highly social, found in constant motion high in the canopy and subcanopy, often in mixed-species foraging flocks. Keeps up a continuous series of thin, whistling and tinkling calls while feeding on blossoms and foliage.
food: Nectar, insects, small berries and soft fruits.
did_you_know: Until 2018 it was known as the Oriental White-eye; that widespread species was then split, with Indian White-eye covering birds from Arabia to Indochina. The white 'spectacles' are rings of minute feathers, not bare skin.

habitat: Extremely adaptable and widespread. Occurs in dry and moist deciduous forest edges, open scrub, agricultural fields, orchards, village groves, roadside avenues and heavily urbanised areas. One of the few native birds that thrives in concrete-dominated cities, provided there are scattered shrubs, small trees or ornamental plantings.

description.adult_male: Medium-sized, dark, crested bulbul. Head, throat and short crest are glossy black; breast and upperparts dark brown with a scaly appearance created by pale feather edges. Underparts grey-brown. The vent (undertail coverts) is a conspicuous crimson-red patch, contrasting with the otherwise dark rear. Tail is blackish with distinct white tips to the outer tail feathers.
description.adult_female: Plumage essentially identical to male; may average slightly smaller and a little duller, but not separable in the field.
description.juvenile: Duller and browner than adults with a sooty-brown head instead of glossy black. Scaling on the breast is less marked. The red vent is initially pale orange or pinkish, becoming brighter with age. Iris slightly darker; gape flanges may be visible at close range.
description.in_flight: Flight is strong, direct and slightly bouncing. From behind, the dark body, flashing white tail-tips and small crimson vent patch are very distinctive as the bird makes short sallies between perches and feeding trees.

behaviour: Bold, noisy and highly adaptable. Freely mixes with human activity in villages, towns and cities. Often perches conspicuously on wires, roof edges and treetops, giving a variety of loud, chattering calls and musical phrases. Aggressive at fruiting and flowering trees, frequently chasing away smaller species such as sunbirds and white-eyes. Roosts communally in dense trees, bamboo clumps or ornamental hedges, arriving at dusk in noisy flocks. Nests are cup-shaped structures placed in shrubs, small trees, creepers or even potted balcony plants.
food: Highly omnivorous. Takes a wide range of fruits and berries (including Lantana, Banyan, Peepal and many garden plants), flower buds and nectar, as well as insects, caterpillars and other small invertebrates. In urban areas readily exploits kitchen scraps and human food waste. An important local seed disperser, but also a prolific consumer of cultivated fruits.

photos.caption: Adult red-vented bulbul

did_you_know: Introduced through the cage-bird trade to Fiji, Hawaii, Samoa and elsewhere, it is the only bird listed among the IUCN's '100 of the World's Worst Invasive Alien Species' for its damage to orchards and native birds.

habitat: Gardens, hedges, scrubland, and forest edges. It prefers low vegetation and is rarely seen high in the canopy. It adapts very well to urban gardens with broad-leaved plants (like crotons or hibiscus) suitable for nesting.

description.adult_male: A tiny, energetic bird with a long, upright tail. Upperparts are bright olive-green; underparts are creamy-white. The forehead and crown are rufous (rust-coloured). Breeding Male Feature: The central two tail feathers become greatly elongated and pin-like, extending well beyond the rest of the tail.
description.adult_female: Similar to the male (rufous crown, olive back) but lacks the elongated central tail feathers. The tail is shorter and rounded.
description.juvenile: Duller overall; the rufous crown is faint or absent (head appears olive-grey). The underparts are washed with yellow.
description.in_flight: Flight is weak and top-heavy due to the long tail. It makes short, jerky dashes between bushes, rarely flying in the open for long.

behaviour: Restless and skulking. It hops among branches with its tail cocked high over its back (wren-like). It is disproportionately loud for its size, giving a loud, rapid, repetitive call 'chu-wee, chu-wee, chu-wee' or 'towit-towit-towit'. Pairs often countersing.
food: Tiny insects, beetles, caterpillars, and nectar (from flowers like Bombax and Erythrina).
did_you_know: To build its nest, it pierces holes in the edges of a large leaf with its beak and sews them together using spider silk or plant fibres, creating a living cradle.

habitat: Woodlands, forest edges, and large urban parks with dense tree cover; in the Western Ghats mostly a winter visitor to wooded hills and plantations.

description.adult_male: Small hawk with blue-grey back and wings, white underparts finely barred with reddish-brown, yellow legs and yellow to orange eyes. Tail long with dark bands.
description.adult_female: Much larger than the male; brown to grey-brown above with brown barring below, yellow eyes and more robust build.
description.juvenile: Brown above, streaked rather than barred below, with yellow eyes; overall more diffuse pattern than adults.
description.in_flight: Short, broad wings and long tail; flies with a distinctive flap-flap-glide action, often low and fast along hedges, tree-lines and forest edges.

behaviour: Quick, agile bird-hunter that relies on surprise, weaving through trees or around buildings to flush small birds. Often seen suddenly dashing across roads or clearings at low height. Tends to be secretive when perched.
food: Small birds primarily; occasionally large insects or small mammals such as mice.
did_you_know: It shows one of the most extreme size differences between the sexes of any bird: females can weigh nearly twice as much as males, and the two hunt prey of different sizes, the small male specialising in tits and finches.

habitat: Freshwater lakes, reservoirs, ponds and slow-moving rivers, often with emergent vegetation and open margins.

description.adult_male: Large grey-brown duck with pale head and neck, dark crown and eye-stripe. Black bill tipped bright yellow with a prominent red spot at the base. Scaly pattern on flanks and white-edged dark speculum.
description.adult_female: Very similar to male; red spot at the bill base may be duller or absent and overall slightly smaller.
description.juvenile: Duller plumage with less contrast on head and neck; bill markings less clear and red spot usually absent.
description.in_flight: Shows white and glossy dark green speculum (wing patch) bordered by white; strong, direct flight with rapid wingbeats.

behaviour: Feeds primarily by dabbling (tipping tail up) in shallow water and by grazing on edges. Less tightly gregarious than some other ducks, often seen in pairs, small groups or loose flocks around village tanks and wetlands.
food: Aquatic vegetation, seeds, grains and small invertebrates such as snails and aquatic insects.
did_you_know: The Eastern Spot-billed Duck of China and Japan, once treated as the same species, lacks the red spots at the base of the bill; the Indian bird's white tertials and green speculum also help set it apart.

habitat: All types of freshwater wetlands, ponds, irrigation tanks, reservoirs and slow rivers; also in mangroves and estuaries.

description.adult_male: Small, slender, glossy black cormorant with relatively short tail and bill. In breeding plumage may show a slight crest and scattered white filoplumes on head and neck.
description.adult_female: Similar to male; sex differences subtle in the field.
description.juvenile: Duller brownish-black with paler throat and breast, giving a two-toned look.
description.in_flight: Flies low and fast over water with steady, shallow wingbeats and neck extended; appears short-tailed compared to larger cormorants.

behaviour: Highly social, often forms large feeding and roosting flocks with other cormorants and herons. Swims low with only head and neck visible, diving frequently to chase fish. Often seen perched on stakes, trees or bunds, wings outstretched to dry.
food: Small fish mainly; also tadpoles and aquatic insects.
did_you_know: The smallest of India's three cormorants, it is told from the Indian Cormorant by its short, stubby bill and flat, squarish head; like all cormorants its plumage wets through when diving, so it must hang its wings out to dry.

habitat: Coastal mudflats, estuaries and large saline or alkaline lakes; in western India often alongside Greater Flamingo.

description.adult_male: Smaller and more delicately built than Greater Flamingo. Plumage typically deeper pink, especially on breast and wing coverts. Bill shorter, darker and more strongly downcurved, with extensive dark maroon-black along the tip and edges.
description.adult_female: Similar to male; slightly smaller with very similar plumage and bill pattern.
description.juvenile: Pale greyish-brown with dull pink only developing gradually; bill pale and less strongly patterned.
description.in_flight: Flies with neck and legs fully extended; wings show dark flight feathers contrasting with pink wing coverts. Flocks form long, wavering lines over water or coast.

behaviour: Feeds in dense flocks, head down and bill inverted, filtering microscopic algae and invertebrates from shallow water. Highly gregarious, often congregating in large flocks where conditions are suitable. In India, more regular at large saline wetlands than deep inland lakes.
food: Algae (especially Spirulina) and other microscopic plant and animal matter filtered from the water.
did_you_know: In India it breeds only on the salt flats of the Rann of Kutch, yet every winter tens of thousands gather in Mumbai's Thane Creek, now a flamingo sanctuary and Ramsar site, filtering the algae that give them their pink colour.

habitat: Paddy fields, marshes, ponds, lakes and river edges; very common in human-dominated landscapes.

description.adult_male: Short-necked heron with dull brown, streaked upperparts and neck when perched, blending well with dry bunds and fields. In flight transforms into a striking white bird because of pure white wings and most of body.
description.adult_female: Similar to male; sexes not easily separated in the field.
description.juvenile: More heavily streaked brown above and below; overall duller and more patterned, with greener bill and legs.
description.in_flight: Completely white wings and most of body except for some brown on back; slow, steady wingbeats and short glides over water or fields.

behaviour: Often sits motionless near edges of water or on bunds, suddenly striking at fish, frogs or insects. Remarkably tame near villages and towns, frequently feeding in flooded fields, roadside pools and small urban tanks.
food: Fish, frogs, crustaceans, aquatic insects and occasionally small reptiles.
did_you_know: Drab for most of the year, it moults into a breeding dress of long white nape plumes and a rich maroon mantle. Its apparent tameness and startling flash of white when flushed have earned it the Hindi name 'andha bagla', the 'blind heron'.

habitat: Lakes, rivers, reservoirs, marshlands and coastal wetlands; favours larger, open waterbodies.

description.adult_male: Large grey heron with long neck, white face, black supercilium extending into black head plumes, and pale grey body. Black shoulder patch, long yellowish bill and dark grey back.
description.adult_female: Similar to male, slightly smaller with slightly shorter head plumes.
description.juvenile: Duller grey overall, lacking the bold black head plumes and with more uniform grey head and neck.
description.in_flight: Slow, deep wingbeats with broad grey wings; neck folded into an S-shape and long legs trailing straight behind.

behaviour: Solitary or in loose groups, stalking fish in shallow water or standing motionless for long periods waiting to strike. Often roosts communally in tall trees near large wetlands and coasts.
food: Fish, frogs, crabs, aquatic insects and small mammals such as rodents.
did_you_know: A specially modified neck vertebra gives the neck its sharp kink and lets the bill strike forward like a released spring. Herons also carry patches of powder down that crumble into a waterproofing dust, which they comb through the plumage with a serrated middle claw.

habitat: Large rivers, reservoirs, lakes and associated sandbars and rocky islets.

description.adult_male: Graceful medium-sized tern with grey upperparts, white underparts, black cap in breeding season and bright yellow bill. Tail long and deeply forked, outer tail feathers slightly longer.
description.adult_female: Identical to male in the field; sexes not easily distinguished.
description.juvenile: Brownish mottling above, paler cap and duller bill; tail fork less pronounced.
description.in_flight: Slender tern with buoyant, agile flight; long narrow wings, deep forked tail and sharp twists and turns over water as it searches for prey.

behaviour: Feeds mainly by plunge-diving into shallow waters from a few metres up, often after hovering briefly. Frequently rests and nests on sandbars, gravel islands or exposed rocks in rivers and reservoirs, sometimes in loose colonies.
food: Small fish, aquatic insects and occasionally crustaceans.
did_you_know: Uplisted to Vulnerable in 2016 after steep declines, it nests on sandbars that are flooded by dam releases, trampled or raided by dogs; one of the largest known colonies is on an island in Karnataka's Bhadra reservoir.

habitat: Deep freshwater lakes, large reservoirs (e.g., Bhigwan, Koyna), and slow-moving rivers. It requires open water for swimming and submerged trees or rocks for drying its wings.

description.adult_male: A large, sleek waterbird with a very long, slender, kinked neck and a dagger-like bill. The body is glossy black; the wings and mantle feature long, silver-grey streaks (often looking like piano keys). A white stripe runs down the side of the neck, bordering the chin. The chin and throat are white.
description.adult_female: Similar to the male, but the neck and breast are pale buff-brown rather than black, fading into a white belly. The silver wing streaks are less contrasting.
description.juvenile: Much paler; the neck and underparts are dirty white or pale buff; the upperparts are brown without the distinct silver streaks.
description.in_flight: In flight, it looks cross-shaped due to its long, thin neck and long, fanned tail. It often soars on thermals high above water, which cormorants rarely do.

behaviour: It swims with its body submerged, leaving only the long, sinuous neck above water, resembling a swimming snake. Unlike cormorants that grab fish, the Darter spears fish with its sharp bill. Its plumage is wettable, which helps it sink and hunt under water, so it must sit with wings spread wide to dry after diving.
food: Almost exclusively fish; occasionally snakes or aquatic invertebrates.
did_you_know: It has a special hinge in its neck vertebrae that allows it to snap its head forward with explosive speed to harpoon fish.

habitat: Dry deciduous forests, open thorn scrub, acacia groves, and mango orchards. In the Sahyadris, it is common on the dry eastern foothills and plateaus, generally avoiding the wet evergreen crests where the Orange Minivet lives.

description.adult_male: A tiny, slender bird with a long tail. The head and back are dark grey (not glossy black like the Orange Minivet). The breast is a soft salmon-orange, deepening to fiery orange on the rump and outer tail feathers. The wings are black with an orange panel.
description.adult_female: Much paler. The upperparts are pale grey. The underparts are off-white or washed with pale yellow (not bright yellow like female Orange Minivets). The rump is dull orange-yellow.
description.juvenile: Resembles the female but has faint barring on the flanks and white tips to the wing coverts.
description.in_flight: Flight is fluttery and hovering. It often hovers like a hummingbird at the tips of branches to pick off insects.

behaviour: Active and restless. Moves in small flocks of 5–10 birds, constantly calling with a thin, high-pitched 'swee-swee'. They forage in the upper canopy of acacia and neem trees. They often join mixed hunting parties with woodshrikes and ioras.
food: Small caterpillars, moths, and beetles.
did_you_know: The male's breast colour can vary from yellow-orange to deep scarlet depending on the subspecies; the Western Ghats race (malabaricus) is particularly vibrant.

habitat: Open scrub, dry stony wastelands, fallow agricultural fields, and outskirts of villages. It avoids dense forests.

description.adult_male: A cryptically patterned bird of grey, brown, and buff, mimicking dead leaves and bark. It has a distinct white patch on either side of the throat (moustachial stripe). In flight, males show expansive white patches near the wing tips and on the outer tail corners.
description.adult_female: Similar camouflage to the male but lacks the large white patches on the wings and tail (these spots are buff or absent).
description.juvenile: Plumage is softer and fluffier with less defined vermiculations; looks like a pale version of the female.
description.in_flight: Silent, erratic, and moth-like flight. It often flies low over cattle or open ground, twisting and turning to catch moths.

behaviour: Strictly nocturnal/crepuscular. During the day, it roosts on the ground, relying on camouflage. It becomes active at dusk, often sitting on dirt roads where its eyes reflect red in headlights ('eye-shine'). Its call is diagnostic: a rhythmic 'chuk-chuk-chuk-chuk-r-r-r', sounding exactly like a stone skipping over ice.
food: Moths, beetles, crickets, and winged termites caught on the wing.
did_you_know: Its generic name Caprimulgus means 'Goatsucker', based on an ancient myth that they suck milk from goats at night: in reality, they just hunt insects attracted to livestock.

habitat: Gardens, farmlands, forest edges, plantations, villages and open countryside; common around human habitation.

description.adult_male: Slim, long-tailed dove with warm grey-brown upperparts and pinkish buff underparts. Most distinctive feature is the black hind-neck patch covered with neat white spots. Long tail has white corners and black subterminal band.
description.adult_female: Very similar to male; may show slightly duller pink tones but not reliably distinguishable.
description.juvenile: Duller brown overall with buff-edged feathers; hind-neck patch poorly formed or absent.
description.in_flight: Fast direct flight with sharp wingbeats; white corners of tail prominent as the tail fans.

behaviour: Usually seen singly, in pairs or loose groups. Feeds mostly on the ground in open areas, often near grain stores or farmland. Walks with deliberate steps. Frequently perches on wires and house roofs. Soft cooing call, a repeated, mellow 'coo-coo-coo'. Generally tame and well adapted to human landscapes.
food: Seeds and grains, small fruits, and occasional insects picked from the ground.
did_you_know: Indian birds of the race suratensis have the black-and-white chequering extending from the nape onto the back, unlike East Asian birds. The species has been introduced to Hawaii, California and Australia, where it is now common in cities.

habitat: Open woodlands, grassy slopes with scattered acacia or scrub, and forest edges. Unlike the Olive-backed Pipit, it avoids deep shade and leaf litter, preferring open grassy patches with clear perches.

description.adult_male: A neat, streaky brown pipit. Upperparts are warm brown with heavy blackish streaking (lacking the greenish-olive tone of the Olive-backed Pipit). The breast is buff with bold black streaks that continue down the flanks as finer lines. The hindclaw is short and curved, unlike the long straight spur of the Paddyfield Pipit. The facial pattern is relatively plain with a weak supercilium.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Upperparts are more scaly; underparts are paler with less distinct streaking.
description.in_flight: Flight is buoyant and undulating. It gives a characteristic, harsh, buzzing call 'teez' or 'speek', which is quite different from the thin whistle of the Olive-backed Pipit.

behaviour: True to its name, it flushes into trees when disturbed, rather than flying far away over the ground like meadow pipits. It walks with a steady gait (not hopping). Before spring migration, males may be heard practicing their song from tree tops.
food: Small insects, weevils, beetles, and grass seeds.
did_you_know: During the breeding season (in the Himalayas/Europe), it performs a spectacular 'parachute' display flight, singing while descending with wings held up in a V-shape.

habitat: Shade-loving. Found in the understorey of evergreen forests, sholas, coffee plantations, and damp wooded ravines. It loves leaf litter and is rarely seen in open sunny grasslands.

description.adult_male: Distinctly greenish-olive above (not warm brown like the Tree Pipit) with faint streaking on the back. Key ID Features: 1) A bold supercilium (eyebrow) that is buff in front of the eye and white behind it. 2) A diagnostic black-and-white spot pattern on the ear coverts (often appearing as two pale spots separated by a dark line). Underparts are whitish with bold black streaks on the breast and flanks.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Browner above with more spotting; less green.
description.in_flight: Flushes silently or with a thin, high-pitched 'tseep' into the mid-canopy of nearby trees. It rarely flies long distances when disturbed.

behaviour: Highly arboreal for a pipit. When flushed, it flies up into a tree and walks along horizontal branches, pumping its tail slowly up and down. On the ground, it is incredibly camouflaged among dead leaves, often allowing a very close approach before exploding upwards.
food: Insects, spiders, and seeds found in forest leaf litter.

photos.caption: Olive-backed Pipit foraging on moss-covered rocks.

did_you_know: It is famously difficult to spot until it moves; its olive-green back matches the shade of the forest floor perfectly.

habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen forests, well-wooded slopes, teak plantations and mixed forest from lowlands to ~1800 m.

description.adult_male: Large, dark woodshrike with ashy grey upperparts, darker grey wings and tail, and a broad black mask through the eye with no pale supercilium. Iris pale yellow. Rump white, striking in flight. Underparts white with a grey wash on the breast.
description.adult_female: Similar to male but browner above, with a duller brownish mask and greyer breast.
description.juvenile: Duller and browner overall with reduced mask; upperparts show slight scaling.
description.in_flight: White rump very prominent; slow, bounding flight through mid-storey and canopy.

behaviour: Usually in pairs or small parties, often perching upright high in the canopy. Gleans insects from leaves and small branches, sometimes sallying short distances. Frequently joins mixed-species flocks in evergreen forest. Call is a loud, ringing, whistled 'twee-tu, twee-tu, twee-tu', along with harsher chattering notes.
food: Insects including caterpillars, beetles and other arthropods gleaned from foliage.
did_you_know: Formerly treated as the Western Ghats race of the Large Woodshrike of the Himalaya and South-east Asia, it was split as a full species on its distinct calls and plumage, making it one of the larger endemic passerines of the Ghats.

habitat: Montane and plateau grasslands, from about 600 m on the northern plateaus to the high sholas of the south, especially wet meadows, marshy depressions, edges of shola patches, reed beds and lush, tall grass on slopes. Strongly associated with saturated grasslands in the southern and central Western Ghats.

description.adult_male: Warm brown upperparts with fine streaking on mantle and a clear buff supercilium. Tail distinctly broad, long, rounded and graduated – with fine dark barring above and dark underside contrasting with pale/white tips. Underparts whitish with buff wash on breast and flanks. Gape black, especially noticeable during singing.
description.adult_female: Structurally identical to male. Plumage similar but gape brown rather than black, and overall tones slightly duller.
description.juvenile: Duller brown with less contrast in tail pattern; buff tones weaker on supercilium and flanks. Underparts more evenly washed buff.
description.in_flight: Male performs characteristic song-flights: fluttering vertical ascent, tail widely fanned to display the broad rounded feathers, combined with a trilling, buzzing call before dropping back suddenly into grass cover. Non-display flight is low and brief.

behaviour: Outside breeding season, extremely skulking – moves mouse-like through dense, wet grass, seldom rising above cover. During breeding, becomes vocal and visible: males ascend in fluttering song-flights with lark-like buzzing trills. Gives sharp 'chack', thin 'tzeep' and metallic 'zink' notes from within grass clumps. Highly site-faithful to specific wet meadows. Distribution patchy and localised despite being resident across suitable high-altitude grasslands.
food: Small insects and arthropods gleaned from grass stems, leaves and ground-level vegetation.

photos.caption: Broad-tailed Grassbird in wet montane grassland, Brahmagiri Wildlife Sanctuary, Karnataka.

did_you_know: Its unusually broad, rounded tail is unique among Asian grassbirds and is displayed dramatically during buzzing song-flights.

habitat: Lowland riparian forests, riverine belts, and moist deciduous forests at the foothills. Unlike the Great Hornbill, it avoids high-altitude rainforests, preferring areas near waterbodies (e.g., Dandeli, Konkan streams).

description.adult_male: A large, pied hornbill. Plumage is glossy black with a white belly, white throat, and white trailing edge to the wings. The massive yellow-and-black casque is shaped like a high, single-bladed axe ('axe-blade' shape), with a large black patch on the front. The outer tail feathers are pure white (not black-tipped), while the central pair is black. The bare skin around the eye is blue-black.
description.adult_female: Similar to the male but smaller. The bare skin around the eye is white or pinkish-flesh coloured (unlike the black skin of the male). The bill and casque are slightly smaller.
description.juvenile: Bill is small and pale yellow; the casque is undeveloped or just a small ridge. The eye patch is pale.
description.in_flight: Flight is laboured and heavy, with a few flaps followed by a glide. The all-white outer tail feathers and the broad white trailing edge of the wings create a striking pattern. The noise of the wings is loud but lacks the heavy 'chugging' sound of the Great Hornbill.

behaviour: Noisy and gregarious. Usually found in pairs or small noisy flocks that congregate at fruiting trees (especially Ficus and Strychnos). Their call is a raucous, shrill, cackling 'kak-kak-kak-kak' that rises in pitch. They are famously fond of riverine habitats and often fly across water channels in the evening to roost.
food: Predominantly frugivorous (figs, drupes); also takes small fish (from drying pools), lizards, and large insects.

photos.caption: Dustbathing times...

did_you_know: The riverine forests around Dandeli in Karnataka hold one of its largest populations and are among the few places where all four Western Ghats hornbills, Great, Malabar Pied, Malabar Grey and Indian Grey, can be seen together.

habitat: Moist deciduous and semi-evergreen forest, forest edges, wooded ravines, hill-station gardens and plantations of the northern and central Western Ghats, from the foothills to about 1,500 m. Most numerous in Maharashtra and Goa, where it replaces the Crimson Sunbird; becomes scarce south of Karnataka.

description.adult_male: Large, long-tailed sunbird with a metallic green crown and moustachial streak, deep crimson head sides, mantle and breast, and a narrow iridescent violet throat. Lower breast and belly dull olive-grey, with fine red streaks on the breast sides. Rump bright yellow, usually hidden. Tail long and metallic blue-green, with the central feathers extended as short points. Bill long, slender and decurved.
description.adult_female: Plain olive-green above and dull yellowish-olive below, slightly brighter on the belly; a faint pale eye-ring and dusky lores. Tail shorter than the male's, dark with pale tips to the outer feathers. Told from female Purple and Purple-rumped Sunbirds by the larger size and longer, more decurved bill.
description.juvenile: Resembles the adult female but duller, greyer below and with a shorter bill. Young males gain scattered crimson and metallic feathers on head and breast during their first moult.
description.in_flight: Fast and direct with whirring wingbeats; the male's red and olive pattern and long pointed tail give a distinctive silhouette. Short dashes between flowering trees, sometimes hovering briefly before a bloom.

behaviour: Usually in pairs, foraging high in flowering trees such as Erythrina, Bombax and Loranthus mistletoes, but also coming low to garden shrubs. Restless and vocal, with a sharp, high 'chee-chee' and a rapid twittering song. Males sing from exposed twigs and chase rivals. The pear-shaped pendant nest of fibres, moss and cobweb is hung from a low branch or creeper, typically during and after the monsoon.
food: Nectar from a wide range of forest and garden flowers; also small insects and spiders, which are gleaned from foliage or taken in short aerial sallies, especially when feeding young.
did_you_know: Long treated as a race of the Crimson Sunbird, it was split on the strength of its larger size, olive belly and much shorter tail streamers. The name honours Nicholas Aylward Vigors, first secretary of the Zoological Society of London.

habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous forest, forest edges, shade-grown coffee and cardamom plantations, and well-wooded gardens throughout the Western Ghats, from the lowlands to about 1,800 m. Commonest in the wetter hills of Kerala, Karnataka and Goa.

description.adult_male: Tiny sunbird, one of the smallest birds in the region. Crown metallic green, throat and upper breast metallic violet-purple bordered below by a crimson breast band; mantle and back crimson, rump metallic purple. Belly pale yellow. Bill short, fine and decurved.
description.adult_female: Olive-brown above with a distinctive dull rufous-red rump, olive-yellow below, brightest on the belly. The reddish rump separates her from other female sunbirds of the region. Bill short and slightly decurved.
description.juvenile: Like the adult female but with a paler rump and yellower underparts; young males soon show patches of crimson on the back and dark feathers on the throat.
description.in_flight: Rapid, buzzing flight on tiny whirring wings; the male's crimson back is conspicuous as it darts between flowers. Often hovers momentarily at blossoms.

behaviour: Singly or in pairs, actively working flowering shrubs and canopy creepers, and frequently joining mixed feeding parties in forest. Males sing a thin, high, rapid trill from exposed perches and give sharp ticking calls. Breeds mainly in the cooler months from around November to March. The small pendant nest of fibres, bark flakes and cobweb is slung from a low branch, often beside a forest path or stream.
food: Nectar from forest flowers, mistletoes and garden plants; also small insects and spiders gleaned from leaves and bark.
did_you_know: At about 8 cm and 4 g it is among the smallest birds in India, and its scientific name minima records that fact.

habitat: Montane grassland on the high plateaus of the Nilgiris, Anamalais and Palani Hills, mostly above 1,500 m, especially tussock grassland on slopes and around shola edges. Absent from the northern Sahyadris. Its range has shrunk with the conversion of grassland to wattle, eucalyptus and tea.

description.adult_male: Richly coloured pipit, warmer than the commoner Paddyfield Pipit. Upperparts rufous-brown with bold dark streaks; breast and flanks washed rich buff with neat dark streaks; belly pale buff. Face buff with a pale eyebrow and a dark moustachial stripe. Tail relatively long with buff, not white, outer feathers. Legs pale pinkish.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: More heavily streaked above and below, with pale fringes to the wing feathers giving a scaly look. Buff tones less warm than in adults.
description.in_flight: Flushes reluctantly and flies a short distance low over the grass before dropping back into cover. The buff outer tail feathers and overall warm tone help separate it from Paddyfield Pipit in flight.

behaviour: Walks and runs through tussocks, often disappearing into grass when approached rather than flying. Less conspicuous than other pipits and seldom perches high. The song, a simple series of thin notes, is given in a short song-flight or from a grass tussock or rock, mainly during the pre-monsoon breeding season. Nests on the ground in a grass cup hidden under a tussock.
food: Insects and other small invertebrates picked from the ground and grass stems; also some grass seeds.
did_you_know: Recent habitat modelling found that less than 500 sq km of suitable montane grassland remains for this pipit, prompting calls to uplist it from Vulnerable to Endangered.

habitat: Open stony hillsides, laterite plateaus, dry grassland, fallow fields, coastal scrub and the edges of cultivation in western India from Gujarat south to Kerala. In the Sahyadris it favours the barren plateau tops and rain-shadow slopes. Near-endemic, confined to western India.

description.adult_male: Compact, rufous-brown crested lark with a long, pointed, often erect crest. Upperparts warm rufous-brown with heavy dark streaking; underparts pale rufous-buff with bold dark streaks across the breast. Rufous outer tail feathers and rufous underwing. Darker and more richly coloured than the Sykes's Lark of the Deccan, with a more heavily streaked breast.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Crest shorter; feathers of the upperparts with pale buff tips and dark subterminal marks, giving a spotted appearance. Breast streaking less distinct.
description.in_flight: Short, fluttering flights low over the ground, showing rufous in the wings and tail. Males perform a fluttering song-flight, rising and hovering before descending.

behaviour: Usually in pairs or small loose groups on open ground, walking and running with the crest raised. Sings a pleasant, rolling series of whistles from a rock, bush-top or in song-flight, mainly before and during the monsoon. Nests in a grass-lined scrape on the ground, often sheltered by a stone or tussock.
food: Seeds, grain and insects, including beetles, grasshoppers and termites, taken from the ground.
did_you_know: It was one of the first Indian birds to receive a scientific name, described by Scopoli in 1786 from specimens collected on the Malabar coast.

habitat: Evergreen and semi-evergreen forest, moist deciduous forest, bamboo and secondary growth along the Western Ghats from Goa south to Kerala and Tamil Nadu, mostly below 1,200 m. Often in the canopy and mid-storey of forest with fruiting trees.

description.adult_male: Handsome, crestless bulbul with a glossy black head and a vivid orange-red throat. Upperparts olive-green; breast and belly bright yellow; wings and tail olive with yellowish edges. Eye pale whitish, bill and legs dark.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Head duller, brownish-black, and the throat patch paler orange-yellow; underparts a less saturated yellow. Eye darker.
description.in_flight: Quick, bouncing flight between trees, the yellow underparts and dark head contrasting clearly. Usually seen flying in loose parties between fruiting trees.

behaviour: Sociable, moving through the canopy in parties of up to a dozen and often joining mixed flocks with other bulbuls and leafbirds. Calls are sweet, bubbling phrases and sharp chattering notes. Feeds mainly in the upper storey but descends to fruiting shrubs at forest edges. Breeds during the monsoon and after, building a small cup nest in a fork or among creepers.
food: Small fruits and berries, including figs and Lantana; also insects and occasionally nectar.
did_you_know: The state bird of Goa, it was long treated as a race of the Black-crested Bulbul before being split, with the yellow-throated birds of Sri Lanka and the Himalaya kept as separate species.

habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous forest, sholas, shade-grown coffee and cardamom plantations and wooded gardens throughout the Western Ghats, from the foothills to around 2,000 m. Also in Sri Lanka. One of the commonest forest bulbuls of the wet hills.

description.adult_male: Bright olive-green above and clear yellow below, with a broad yellow eyebrow and yellow eye-ring on an olive face. Crown unstreaked and crestless. Eye reddish-brown; bill dark; legs greyish. Larger and more richly yellow than any leaf warbler and with a heavier bill.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Duller, with a browner wash to the upperparts and paler yellow underparts; the eyebrow less distinct.
description.in_flight: Direct, slightly undulating flight through the understorey and mid-storey, showing bright yellow underparts and olive wings.

behaviour: Active and noisy, in pairs or small groups in the lower and middle storeys, regularly joining mixed hunting parties. Calls include loud, cheerful whistled phrases and harsh scolding notes. Gleans insects from foliage and takes fruit from shrubs and small trees. Breeds mainly from the pre-monsoon into the monsoon, building a neat cup of leaves and moss bound with cobweb in a low fork.
food: Berries, figs and other small fruits, insects, spiders and some nectar.
did_you_know: It is the only member of its genus, Acritillas, and its nearest relatives are the brown bulbuls of Southeast Asia rather than the familiar Pycnonotus bulbuls of gardens.

habitat: Evergreen forest, sholas and shade plantations of the Western Ghats, mostly in the hills above 600 m, and in Sri Lanka. Most numerous in the higher ranges of Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka; scarcer in the northern Sahyadris.

description.adult_male: Large, slender, dark slaty-grey bulbul with a blacker head and a loose, ragged crest of elongated crown feathers. Wings and tail blackish, the tail only slightly notched. Bill, legs and feet bright orange-red, the eye dark. Sometimes called Black Bulbul.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Browner and paler, with whitish tips to the wing coverts; bill and legs duller orange-brown.
description.in_flight: Strong, direct flight high over the canopy in noisy, straggling flocks, the dark plumage and red bill obvious. Often crosses valleys and clearings in parties.

behaviour: Gregarious and noisy, roaming the canopy in flocks that may number dozens outside the breeding season and gathering at fruiting and flowering trees. Calls are loud, nasal, squealing and mewing notes, constantly repeated. Takes insects in aerial sallies from treetops. Breeds during the early monsoon, building a cup nest of moss and lichen in a canopy fork.
food: Fruits and berries, including figs and wild cinnamon; nectar from flowering trees; also beetles and other insects caught in flight.
did_you_know: It was formerly lumped with the Himalayan Black Bulbul, and was split partly on the basis of its much less forked tail, which gave it its present English name.

habitat: Shola forest, shola edges, dense scrub, tea estates and hill-station gardens above about 1,100 m in the Palani Hills, Anamalai Hills and the High Ranges around Munnar, south of the Palghat Gap. Tolerates secondary growth and garden hedges more than its relatives.

description.adult_male: Olive-brown laughingthrush with a dark grey-brown crown, a narrow dark eyestripe and a broad white eyebrow that extends well behind the eye. Throat and upper breast grey, shading to rusty-brown on the lower breast, belly and flanks. Wings and tail olive-brown. Eye reddish, bill black.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Duller, with a less contrasting eyebrow and a browner, less clearly grey breast.
description.in_flight: Short, low, whirring flights between bushes or across a gap in the shola; seldom flies far. The rounded wings and longish tail give a typical laughingthrush shape.

behaviour: Lively and inquisitive, in pairs or small groups moving through undergrowth and low trees, often close to the ground. Bold around hill-station gardens, where it visits bird tables and ornamental shrubs. Calls are loud, ringing whistles, often given in duet, and harsh chattering. Breeds mainly from February to June, building a cup nest of moss and rootlets in a dense bush.
food: Insects, berries, small fruits and nectar; also flower petals and scraps around habitation.
did_you_know: It was named after Samuel Fairbank, an American missionary who collected the type specimen in the Palani Hills in the 1860s.

habitat: Shola forest and adjoining dense scrub on a handful of isolated peaks between 1,400 and 2,400 m from the Brahmagiri Hills in Kodagu south through Banasura Hill, Chembra Peak and Vellarimala in Wayanad and Kozhikode. Total range is under 60 sq km.

description.adult_male: Olive-brown laughingthrush with a black face, chin and throat and a clean white eyebrow. Cheeks, breast and nape grey, contrasting with an ochre belly and olive-brown wings and tail. Eye crimson, bill black, legs brownish. The grey breast and black chin separate it from the other Montecincla species.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Duller, with the black of the throat less extensive and the grey breast washed brown.
description.in_flight: Brief, low flights between patches of shola undergrowth, rarely crossing open ground.

behaviour: Skulks in pairs or small parties in dense shola understorey and bracken, coming into the open to feed at fruiting shrubs or along forest edges in the early morning. Calls are loud, clear whistles and chattering, given in duet by pairs. Breeds in the pre-monsoon months, nesting low in dense shrubs.
food: Insects, berries and small fruits, and nectar from shola flowers such as Rhododendron and Strobilanthes.
did_you_know: Confined to a few peaks around Wayanad, its estimated world population is only 500 to 2,500 adults, making it one of the most range-restricted birds in mainland India.

habitat: Shola forest, shola edges, dense scrub and tea estate margins above about 1,000 m in the Ashambu (Agasthyamalai) Hills and neighbouring ranges of southern Kerala and Tamil Nadu, south of the Shencottah Gap.

description.adult_male: Very like the Palani Laughingthrush: olive-brown above with a dark crown, grey throat and upper breast and rusty-brown belly. The diagnostic feature is the very short white eyebrow, which stops in front of the eye rather than extending behind it. Eye reddish, bill black.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Duller and browner, with the short eyebrow even less distinct.
description.in_flight: Short, low flights between bushes and shola patches; rarely seen in the open.

behaviour: Pairs and small groups work through dense undergrowth and low trees, often near the ground, and join mixed flocks at shola edges. Vocal, with loud whistled duets and harsh chatters. Breeding is during the pre-monsoon and early monsoon, with a cup nest placed low in a dense shrub.
food: Insects, small fruits and berries, and nectar.
did_you_know: Three laughingthrushes, Palani, Banasura and Ashambu, were split from one species in 2017 after genetic work showed that populations on separate mountain blocks had been isolated long enough to become distinct.

habitat: Moist and dry deciduous forest, evergreen forest edges, bamboo, scrub, teak plantations and the edges of cultivation throughout the Western Ghats and peninsular India, from the plains to about 2,000 m. Confined to India, where it replaces the Red Junglefowl south and west of the Narmada.

description.adult_male: Large, grey fowl with a red comb and wattles, a bare red face and a long, drooping, glossy black-green sickle tail. Neck and mantle feathers grey with striking yellow and white spangled tips, giving a spotted 'necklace'; body finely vermiculated grey. Legs reddish with long spurs. About 70 to 80 cm including the tail.
description.adult_female: Much smaller and plainer, about 38 cm. Brown above with fine pale streaks, whitish below with bold black scaling on the breast and flanks; no comb or wattles. Legs pale.
description.juvenile: Resembles the female but duller and more streaked; young males begin to show grey vermiculations and spangled neck feathers within their first months.
description.in_flight: Bursts up noisily when flushed and flies strongly for a short distance on rounded wings before gliding into cover. The male's long tail trails behind.

behaviour: Shy and alert, feeding in the early morning and late afternoon along forest roads and clearings, and retreating into thick cover when disturbed. Usually a cock with one or two hens, or small parties outside the breeding season. The cock's crow is a loud, distinctive 'kuk-kaya-kaya-kuk', very different from the domestic cockerel, given from the ground or a roost tree. Roosts in trees. Nests on the ground in a scrape under a bush or bamboo clump.
food: Seeds, grain, bamboo seed, fallen fruit, tubers, termites and other insects, scratched from leaf litter and forest floor.
did_you_know: The yellow gene of domestic chickens was inherited from the Grey Junglefowl, which shows that early domestic fowl, descended mainly from the Red Junglefowl, hybridised with this species.

habitat: Aerial over forest, hills, plantations, coastal plains and offshore islets along the Western Ghats from Maharashtra to Kerala, and in Sri Lanka. Breeds colonially in sea caves, cliff crevices, tunnels and rock overhangs, with the largest colonies on islands off the Konkan and Malabar coasts.

description.adult_male: Small, dull swift, uniform grey-brown above with a slightly paler, greyish rump, and pale grey-brown below. Tail short and only slightly notched. Wings long, narrow and scythe-shaped. Bill tiny, eye dark.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Indistinguishable in the field from adults.
description.in_flight: Fluttering, bat-like flight with quick wingbeats interspersed with short glides, often in loose flocks low over forest canopy, rivers and reservoirs. Smaller and weaker-flying than Asian Palm Swift and lacking the deeply forked tail.

behaviour: Almost entirely aerial, feeding in flocks from dawn to dusk and often joining other swifts and swallows over water or before rain. Roosts and breeds in dark caves, where it navigates by echolocation using audible clicks. Nests are small half-cups of saliva mixed with moss and feathers glued to cave walls, built in colonies that can number thousands. Breeds mainly from February to June.
food: Small flying insects such as flies, flying ants and termites, caught on the wing.
did_you_know: Its saliva nests were once harvested for the bird's-nest soup trade on the Vengurla Rocks off Maharashtra, and colonies there are now protected.

habitat: Dry and moist deciduous forest with teak, open canopy and dense undergrowth in the Satpura range and the northern Western Ghats. Known populations in Melghat and Toranmal in Maharashtra, the Tapi valley and, since 2014, Tansa Wildlife Sanctuary in the northern Sahyadris near Mumbai. Also recorded in Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Chhattisgarh and Odisha.

description.adult_male: Small, stocky, day-active owl with a large, rather flat head and short tail. Upperparts dark greyish-brown with very little spotting on the crown and mantle, unlike the heavily spotted Spotted Owlet. Underparts white with a broad, dark-barred breast band and bold dark bars on the flanks. Wings and tail strongly banded. Facial disc pale with dark rims; eyes yellow; legs feathered white with large, strong feet.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike, the female slightly larger.
description.juvenile: Paler and softer-plumaged, with a greyer, more uniform crown and fainter barring below.
description.in_flight: Short, direct flights between perches with rapid wingbeats, showing boldly barred wings and tail. Often moves in full daylight.

behaviour: Strongly diurnal, hunting from exposed perches on bare branches and tree-tops, even in the heat of the day. Watches for prey and drops to the ground or pounces in low vegetation. Calls include a soft 'uh-wuww' and a loud, whistled 'kwaak kwaak' territorial call, given mainly in the cool season. Pairs defend territories year-round and nest in natural tree cavities, with eggs laid from about October to December. Tail is frequently flicked and wagged when the bird is alert.
food: Lizards, skinks, frogs, rodents, small birds and large insects; a higher proportion of vertebrate prey than the Spotted Owlet, taken with its powerful feet.
did_you_know: Known from only seven specimens collected before 1884, it was presumed extinct until Pamela Rasmussen rediscovered it in 1997 near Shahada, Maharashtra. Her work also exposed that a museum specimen supposedly collected in Gujarat had been relabelled by Richard Meinertzhagen.

habitat: Tall evergreen and moist deciduous forest of the Western Ghats, mainly in the hills from about 300 to 2,000 m, with some seasonal movement to lower elevations in search of fruiting trees. Also found in the Himalaya and Southeast Asia.

description.adult_male: Very large, heavy pigeon with a pale grey head and underparts, the neck and breast washed pinkish, and a dark maroon-brown back and wings. Tail blackish with a broad pale grey terminal band, obvious from below. Undertail coverts buff. Bill red at the base with a pale tip; eye pale with a red orbital ring; legs red.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike, the female very slightly duller.
description.juvenile: Duller, with the maroon of the upperparts browner and the grey of the head tinged brown; bare parts paler.
description.in_flight: Powerful, direct flight on broad wings, with slow, deep wingbeats; noticeably larger and heavier than Green Imperial Pigeon, with a dark back and the pale band across the tail tip visible from below. Often crosses valleys high over the canopy.

behaviour: Singly, in pairs or small groups in the canopy of tall fruiting trees, where it perches quietly and can be hard to see despite its size. The call is a deep, booming, far-carrying 'wuh-wooom', often the first sign of the bird's presence. Performs a display flight, rising steeply then stalling and gliding down. Nests on a flimsy platform of twigs in a tall tree, laying a single egg, mainly from the early monsoon to the cool season.
food: Fruits, especially figs, wild nutmeg, laurels and other large-seeded forest fruits, swallowed whole; an important disperser of large forest seeds.
did_you_know: Its booming call is so deep that it is sometimes mistaken for a distant animal; the bird can swallow fruits up to the size of a small plum and pass the seed intact.

habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous forest, forest edges, shade-grown coffee and cardamom, and tall trees around forest villages along the Western Ghats from about Goa south to Kerala and Tamil Nadu, and in Sri Lanka. Mostly in the foothills and mid-elevations.

description.adult_male: Glossy purple-black myna with a bright orange-yellow bill, yellow legs and bright yellow fleshy wattles on the nape that extend forward below the eye as a thin yellow line. A bold white wing patch is formed by the bases of the primaries. Smaller than the Common Hill Myna of the north-east, with a slimmer bill and the nape wattles meeting the eye wattle.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Duller, browner black with less gloss, the wattles smaller and paler and the bill duller yellow.
description.in_flight: Fast, direct flight with rapid wingbeats, the white wing patches flashing conspicuously. Usually in pairs or small parties flying over the canopy.

behaviour: Pairs or small groups perch high in tall trees, often on bare branches, and gather in larger numbers at fruiting figs. Extremely vocal, with loud, varied whistles, shrieks and liquid notes, the birds often calling in duet. Nests in tree holes, frequently in a dead tree in a clearing, during the pre-monsoon and monsoon months.
food: Fruits and berries, especially figs; also nectar from flowering trees such as Bombax and Erythrina, and some insects.
did_you_know: Its fame as a mimic in captivity has driven a long history of trapping for the cage-bird trade, and its wild populations are considered to be declining.

habitat: Moist deciduous and evergreen forest, teak plantations, bamboo and shade-grown coffee along the Western Ghats from Maharashtra south to Kerala, mainly in the foothills and mid-elevations. Also occurs in central and north-east India and Southeast Asia.

description.adult_male: Small, oddly proportioned woodpecker with a large head, prominent pointed black crest and a very short tail. Crown and crest black; face, throat and a broad band across the neck buffy white; back and wings black with bold heart-shaped black spots on the white tertials and wing coverts. Underparts dark olive-grey. Rump white, usually hidden. Bill short and dark.
description.adult_female: Similar to the male but with the forehead and forecrown buffy white rather than black.
description.juvenile: Duller, with the black areas browner and the heart-shaped markings less crisp.
description.in_flight: Fast, deeply undulating flight; the large head, stubby tail and white rump give a distinctive, almost tailless silhouette.

behaviour: In pairs or small family groups, and a regular member of mixed hunting flocks. Forages on thin outer branches and twigs in the canopy rather than on trunks, often hanging acrobatically. Calls include a sharp 'kee-kee-kee' and a chattering trill; also drums briefly. Nests in a small hole excavated in a dead branch or stub, mostly from the cool season to the pre-monsoon.
food: Ants, termites, beetle larvae and other insects gleaned from bark and foliage; also takes small fruits.
did_you_know: It has a patch of specialised feathers on its lower back that secrete a sticky, scented substance, a feature unique to its genus whose function is still not understood.

habitat: Shaded streams and pools inside dense evergreen and moist deciduous forest along the Western Ghats from Goa and Karnataka south to Kerala and Tamil Nadu, mainly below 1,000 m. Rare and local north of Goa. Avoids open water, unlike the Common Kingfisher.

description.adult_male: Small, jewel-like kingfisher, very like the Common Kingfisher but with the ear coverts blue rather than rufous, deeper, more cobalt-blue upperparts with a paler blue stripe down the back, and richer orange-rufous underparts. Bill all black. Lacks the rufous cheek patch of Common Kingfisher.
description.adult_female: Similar to the male but with the lower mandible reddish at the base.
description.juvenile: Duller, with rufous ear coverts like Common Kingfisher, a dusky wash across the breast and a pale-tipped orange-based bill; easily confused at this age.
description.in_flight: Very fast, direct, low flight along forest streams, appearing as a flash of intense blue; darker and deeper blue than Common Kingfisher.

behaviour: Shy and easily overlooked, perching motionless on a low, shaded branch or root over a forest stream, often in deep gloom, and darting away at the first disturbance. Dives for small fish and aquatic insects from the perch. Call is a high, thin 'tsit', shriller and shorter than Common Kingfisher's. Nests in a tunnel in a stream bank, mainly during the monsoon.
food: Small fish, tadpoles, aquatic insects, crustaceans and small frogs, caught by diving from a low perch.
did_you_know: Its deep blue ear coverts are the surest way to tell it from the Common Kingfisher, but juveniles have rufous cheeks and are best separated by their darker upperparts and forest-stream habitat.

habitat: Dense undergrowth, bamboo, reeds and bracken in evergreen and moist deciduous forest, forest edges and shade plantations along the Western Ghats from about Maharashtra south to Kerala and Tamil Nadu, and in Sri Lanka. Most common in the wetter hills, from the foothills to around 2,000 m.

description.adult_male: Small, plump babbler with a dark blackish-brown hood covering the crown, face and ear coverts, a pale whitish eye that stands out from the dark head, and rufous-brown upperparts. Throat and underparts white with a buffy wash on the flanks. Tail short and rounded. Bill dark, legs pale.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Hood browner and less extensive, eye darker, underparts washed buff.
description.in_flight: Weak, whirring flights of a few metres between bushes, low to the ground, with the flock crossing gaps one bird at a time.

behaviour: In restless parties of five to a dozen birds that move quickly through thick cover near the ground, keeping in touch with constant harsh, churring and rattling calls. Skulking but inquisitive, responding to squeaking and pishing. Often the core of understorey mixed flocks with tailorbirds and warblers. Builds a domed nest of leaves and grass low in a bush or bamboo, breeding mainly during the monsoon.
food: Insects, spiders and other small invertebrates gleaned from leaves and stems in the undergrowth; occasionally berries.
did_you_know: Its pale eye glowing from a dark hood is the best field mark; the eye changes from dark in juveniles to almost white in adults.

habitat: Evergreen and moist deciduous forest on steep hill slopes and ridges throughout the Western Ghats, from the foothills to the highest sholas. Usually seen quartering slowly over forested valleys and along escarpments. Widespread in the hills of South and Southeast Asia.

description.adult_male: Large, all-black eagle with very long, broad wings that are distinctly paddle-shaped, widest at the hand, and a long tail. Cere and feet bright yellow, contrasting with the black plumage. Faint greyish barring on the tail and flight feathers. Eye dark.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike, the female slightly larger.
description.juvenile: Dark brown rather than black, with buff-streaked underparts and head, paler fringes to the upperparts and more obvious barring on the wings and tail. Cere and feet yellow as in adults.
description.in_flight: Unmistakable: glides and soars slowly on long wings held in a shallow V, with the primaries splayed and upcurved like fingers and the tail often spread. Flies very slowly and buoyantly just above the canopy, tilting and checking as it searches the treetops. Black plumage with yellow feet visible at close range.

behaviour: Spends much of the day hunting on the wing, drifting low over the canopy and along forested ridges in a slow, controlled flight that allows it to inspect the treetops for nests. Will hang almost motionless in updraughts. Usually silent, but gives a shrill, plaintive 'kee-kee' in display. Pairs soar together and perform undulating display flights over the breeding territory. Builds a large stick nest in a tall forest tree, breeding mainly from November to March.
food: Eggs and nestlings of birds, frequently taking whole nests; also small mammals including squirrels and bats, lizards, and large insects, snatched from the canopy.
did_you_know: Its outer toes and claws are less curved than those of other eagles, an adaptation thought to help it grasp and carry away entire birds' nests, which it raids for eggs and chicks.

habitat: Open country, farmland, grassland, scrub, village surroundings, plantations and forest edges throughout the Western Ghats and lowlands; avoids dense forest interior, where it is replaced by Bronzed and Ashy Drongos. Common around grazing cattle and along roadside wires.

description.adult_male: Glossy black drongo with a long, deeply forked tail, the outer feathers slightly splayed outwards. Small white spot at the base of the bill, present in most adults. Bill stout and black, eye dark reddish-brown. Duller and blacker than Bronzed Drongo, larger and with a deeper fork than Ashy Drongo.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Browner and less glossy, with whitish scaling on the belly and undertail coverts and a shallower tail fork.
description.in_flight: Agile and acrobatic, with sudden twists and dives when chasing insects; sallies from perches and returns. The deeply forked tail is conspicuous. Will pursue crows, kites and other larger birds with fearless aggression.

behaviour: Conspicuous and bold, perching upright on wires, fence posts, bare branches and even the backs of cattle, from which it sallies after insects disturbed by grazing animals or ploughing. Fiercely territorial when breeding, attacking crows, raptors and other intruders far larger than itself. Calls are harsh, grating and chattering, with some mimicry. Gathers at grass fires and swarming termites. Nests in a shallow cup in a high fork, breeding mainly from April to August.
food: Grasshoppers, beetles, dragonflies, termites, moths and other insects; occasionally small birds, lizards and nectar from flowering trees.
did_you_know: Smaller birds such as doves and orioles often nest near Black Drongos, benefiting from the drongos' aggressive defence of their territory against crows and raptors.

habitat: Open water of all kinds: rivers, reservoirs, irrigation tanks, canals, estuaries, creeks and coastal backwaters throughout the lowlands and foothills of the Western Ghats. Scarce in the forested interior and at higher elevations, where clear open water is limited. Widespread across Africa and southern Asia.

description.adult_male: Unmistakable black-and-white kingfisher with a shaggy black crest, a long, heavy black bill and a broad white supercilium. Upperparts black, boldly spotted and barred with white; underparts white with two black breast bands, the upper one broad and complete, the lower narrower and often broken.
description.adult_female: Similar to the male but with a single black breast band, usually broken in the centre.
description.juvenile: Like the female but duller, with a greyish wash and fine dark scaling on the throat and breast, and a brownish tinge to the black upperparts.
description.in_flight: Strong, direct flight low over the water on rapid wingbeats, the black-and-white wings and tail strikingly patterned. Habitually hovers with the body held near vertical and the bill pointing down, before plunging headlong.

behaviour: The most conspicuous kingfisher of open water, fishing by hovering steadily some metres above the surface, often for many seconds, then diving. Also hunts from perches on posts, rocks and overhead wires. Usually in pairs or small family groups, and sociable where prey is plentiful, with several birds fishing together. Call is a sharp, chattering 'chirruk chirruk', given frequently in flight. Nests in a tunnel in a sandy river bank or cutting, breeding mainly from November to April; young from earlier broods and other adults sometimes help at the nest.
food: Small fish, taken mainly by hovering and plunge-diving; also aquatic insects, tadpoles, frogs and crustaceans. Small prey is swallowed in flight, allowing the bird to feed far from any perch.
did_you_know: It is one of the largest birds capable of sustained hovering, and by swallowing small fish on the wing it can fish over large lakes and estuaries where there are no perches at all.

habitat: Open woodland, dry and moist deciduous forest, scrub, thorn forest, farmland, plantations, gardens and towns, from the plains into the lower hills of the Western Ghats. Much less common in dense evergreen forest and in the wettest high hills, where Purple-rumped, Crimson-backed and Vigors's Sunbirds predominate.

description.adult_male: In breeding plumage appears all black at a distance, but in good light glossy metallic purple-blue over the entire head, upperparts and breast, with a narrow maroon band across the breast and dark blackish belly. Small yellow and orange tufts at the sides of the breast are usually hidden. Bill long, thin and decurved, black. In non-breeding or eclipse plumage, mainly from around June to November, the male resembles the female but retains a broad glossy purple-black stripe down the centre of the throat and breast and dark blue-black wings and tail.
description.adult_female: Dull olive-brown above with a faint pale supercilium, and uniform pale yellow below. Tail blackish with white tips to the outer feathers. Told from the female Purple-rumped Sunbird by the yellow rather than grey throat and the lack of any grey on the breast.
description.juvenile: Like the female; young males soon begin to show dark blotches on the throat and breast as the glossy feathers come through.
description.in_flight: Fast, darting flight between flowering shrubs and trees, and frequently hovers briefly in front of flowers, particularly when the corolla offers no perch.

behaviour: Active and noisy, singly or in pairs, working rapidly through flowering trees and shrubs and probing blossoms with the long bill. Often pierces the base of large or tubular flowers to reach the nectar. Males sing a rapid, twittering 'cheewit-cheewit' from an exposed twig and give a sharp 'chwit' call. Builds a pear-shaped pouch nest of fibres, bark and cobwebs with a side entrance, suspended from a low branch or even from wires and verandah plants, mainly from February to June in the region; only the female builds and incubates.
food: Nectar from a wide range of flowering plants, including Erythrina, Bombax, Butea, Calotropis, Woodfordia and many garden species; also small insects and spiders, especially when feeding young.
did_you_know: Unlike most Indian sunbirds, the male Purple Sunbird moults into a drab eclipse plumage after breeding, looking much like the female except for a dark stripe down the throat and breast.

habitat: Open woodland, deciduous forest, forest edges, orchards, plantations, farmland with scattered trees, village groves, gardens and city parks throughout the plains and foothills of the Western Ghats. Follows its crow hosts into towns and is scarce only in dense evergreen forest and on the highest plateaus.

description.adult_male: Large, slim, long-tailed cuckoo, entirely glossy blue-black with a stout pale greenish bill and a striking crimson eye. Legs grey. Superficially crow-like, but the slender shape, long graduated tail and red eye are distinctive.
description.adult_female: Very different: dark brown above, densely spotted and barred with white and buff, with the crown streaked and the wings and tail barred; underparts whitish, heavily barred dark brown. Eye crimson, bill pale green.
description.juvenile: Resembles the female but browner and more uniformly barred, with a dark eye. Young males soon show patches of black.
description.in_flight: Direct flight with steady wingbeats, the long tail evident; usually seen dashing between tree canopies, often pursued by crows.

behaviour: Shy and skulking despite its size, keeping within dense foliage and far more often heard than seen. The male's loud, rising 'ko-el, ko-el' call, repeated with increasing pitch and urgency, dominates the pre-monsoon months from March to June, and is heard day and night; the female gives a shrill, bubbling 'kik-kik-kik'. A brood parasite that in India lays its eggs mainly in the nests of House and Large-billed Crows; the male often distracts the crows while the female slips in to lay. Unlike many cuckoos, the koel chick does not usually evict its nest mates, and both koel and crow young may fledge from the same nest.
food: Mainly fruits and berries, especially figs, and also mulberries, papaya and other cultivated fruit; also caterpillars, other insects and occasionally eggs of small birds. An important disperser of fig and other tree seeds.
did_you_know: The koel's eggs resemble those of its crow hosts, and its chicks often grow up alongside crow nestlings rather than pushing them out, so the foster parents may raise both.

habitat: Open woodland, dry and moist deciduous forest, groves, orchards, roadside avenues, gardens and city parks, from the plains into the foothills of the Western Ghats. Favours areas with fig trees and dead branches for nesting. Largely absent from dense evergreen forest and the higher hills, where White-cheeked and Malabar Barbets take its place.

description.adult_male: Small, dumpy, bright green barbet with a short, thick bill. Crimson forehead and a crimson patch on the upper breast, separated by a yellow throat; bright yellow patches above and below the eye set in a black face. Underparts pale yellowish-green with heavy dark green streaking. Legs and feet reddish.
description.adult_female: Sexes alike.
description.juvenile: Duller, lacking the crimson on the forehead and breast, which are replaced by dull green and yellow; face pattern more subdued.
description.in_flight: Direct, slightly undulating flight on whirring wings, appearing green and stubby; often flies some distance between fruiting trees.

behaviour: Best known for its monotonous, metallic 'tuk, tuk, tuk' call, delivered for minutes on end from a bare treetop, the bird bobbing its head and jerking its tail with each note; several birds often call at once. Calls mainly in the hot months but may be heard year-round. Singly or in pairs, and in groups at fruiting figs. Excavates a small nest hole in a dead branch or soft-wooded trunk, often on the underside of a bough, breeding chiefly from December to June. Both sexes dig the hole and feed the young.
food: Fruits and berries, above all figs, together with other soft fruits such as those of Lantana and mulberry; also takes insects, especially winged termites, and occasionally flower petals.
did_you_know: Its name comes from its call, a steady metallic 'tuk, tuk, tuk' likened to a coppersmith hammering a sheet of metal, and the bird may repeat the note more than a hundred times a minute.

habitat: Gardens, villages, towns, farmland, orchards, open woodland, forest edges and plantations throughout the Western Ghats lowlands and hills, up to the hill stations. One of the most familiar birds around human habitation, but scarce inside dense, unbroken evergreen forest.

description.adult_male: Neat black-and-white chat with a glossy blue-black head, breast and upperparts, white belly and vent, a long white wing bar and a long black tail with white outer feathers. Bill and legs black. Stands upright with the tail often cocked.
description.adult_female: Pattern as in the male but the black replaced by dark slaty grey, especially on the throat and breast; the white belly is tinged greyish.
description.juvenile: Like the female but browner, with the throat and breast mottled and scaled buff-brown.
description.in_flight: Short, low flights between the ground and perches, the white wing bar and white outer tail feathers flashing; rarely flies far.

behaviour: Confiding and conspicuous, hopping on lawns, paths and ploughed fields and flicking up its tail, or singing from a rooftop, post or treetop. The song, given especially at dawn and dusk in the breeding season, is a rich, varied series of clear whistled phrases, often including imitations of other birds; also a harsh 'chrr' scold and a plaintive rising whistle. Males are strongly territorial, raising the tail and puffing out the feathers in display and in disputes with neighbours. Nests in a tree hole, wall crevice, pipe or nest box, breeding mainly from March to July.
food: Mainly insects and other invertebrates, including beetles, grasshoppers, caterpillars, ants and earthworms, picked from the ground and low vegetation; occasionally small geckos, nectar and berries.
did_you_know: Though popularly called a robin, it is a chat in the flycatcher family, and it is the national bird of Bangladesh, where it is known as the doyel.

habitat: Dry and moist deciduous forest, bamboo, thorn scrub with trees, shaded ravines, plantations, overgrown orchards and wooded gardens, from the plains into the foothills of the Western Ghats. Prefers drier, more open woodland than the Blue-throated Flycatcher and is often found near streams in the dry season.

description.adult_male: Small, long-tailed flycatcher with bright blue upperparts, head and tail, the forehead and shoulder paler, brighter blue. Throat and breast rich orange-rufous, grading sharply into a clean white belly. Lores blackish. Bill and legs dark.
description.adult_female: Duller, with the blue of the upperparts replaced by greyish-blue and the crown and mantle tinged brown; tail and wings bluish. Throat and breast paler orange than the male, belly white.
description.juvenile: Brown above and buff below, heavily spotted and scaled with pale buff and dark brown, with bluish wings and tail.
description.in_flight: Short, quick sallies from a low perch after flying insects, returning to the same or a nearby perch; the blue tail is spread and flicked on landing.

behaviour: Quiet and unobtrusive, perching upright in the shade of the middle and lower storey, from where it makes brief sallies or drops to the ground for insects. Singly or in pairs, and sometimes with mixed flocks. The song is a short, sweet, descending trill of six to ten clear notes, often given through the heat of the day when few other birds are calling; also a sharp 'tik' and a harsh churr. Nests in a cup of moss and rootlets in a hollow, rock crevice or bank, or among roots, breeding mainly from April to August.
food: Small insects, including flies, beetles, moths and caterpillars, taken in the air and from foliage and the ground.
did_you_know: It is named after Samuel Tickell, a nineteenth-century army officer and naturalist in India, and is the only one of the region's blue-and-orange flycatchers with a white belly sharply cut off from the orange breast.
